entry.sum: Singular cohomology $H^n(X;G)$ is the cohomology of the cochain complex $\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(X),G)$ of functions on singular simplices. It is a contravariant homotopy invariant with long exact sequences, excision and Mayer–Vietoris, and the universal coefficient theorem computes it from homology. The cup product makes $H^*(X;R)$ a graded-commutative ring, which distinguishes spaces with the same homology groups, such as the torus and $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$.
entry.why: Cohomology is where products, characteristic classes, obstructions and duality live; its ring structure is the first invariant that sees how cycles intersect, and it is the input to spectral sequences, K-theory and the cochain-level algorithms of data analysis and lattice physics.

links.note: Lattice models of topological phases are written with Z/2 cochains on a triangulation, their cup products and Steenrod's higher cup-i products.
Persistent cup-length and circular coordinates in topological data analysis are computed from explicit simplicial cocycles and cup products.

blocks.body:
Glue two circles and a sphere at a single point. The resulting space $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$ has the same homology groups as the torus $T^2$: $\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0$ and $2$ and $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in degree $1$. Yet the two spaces are not homotopy equivalent. On the torus the two basic loops are forced to cross; on the wedge they meet only at the base point and can be pushed apart. Homology groups cannot see this, because homology has no natural way to multiply two classes.

Cohomology dualises homology. A $k$-cochain is a function that assigns a number to every $k$-simplex, and its coboundary records how it fails to be consistent across the $(k+1)$-simplices. Two features make the dual theory worth having. It is contravariant: a map $f\colon X\to Y$ pulls cochains on $Y$ back to cochains on $X$, as functions are pulled back. And cochains can be multiplied: the cup product of a $k$-cochain and an $l$-cochain is a $(k+l)$-cochain, and on cohomology it makes $H^*(X;R)$ a graded ring. On the torus the product of the two degree-one classes generates $H^2$; on the wedge every such product is zero. Contessoto et al. use exactly this pair to show that cup products distinguish data sets that ordinary persistent homology cannot, and the Wikipedia survey states the moral: the ring is usually a stronger invariant than the groups.

After working through this page you will be able to compute cohomology groups directly from cochains, or from homology by the universal coefficient theorem; compute cup products on a triangulated space by hand, as data-analysis and lattice-physics papers do; use the Künneth theorem, graded commutativity and naturality to determine cohomology rings of tori, surfaces and projective spaces; and use the rings to prove that spaces and maps are different.

The page assumes [[homology]] (chains, $\partial\partial=0$, singular homology and its properties), the long exact sequence and five lemma of [[homological-algebra]], and Ext from [[ext]]. Historically, the cup product grew out of the intersection theory of Alexander and Lefschetz in the 1920s; Kolmogorov and Alexander introduced cohomology in 1935, Čech and Whitney developed cup products for finite complexes in 1936–38, and Eilenberg gave the singular definition used here in 1944. Poincaré duality for topological manifolds, with orientations and cap products, is a separate topic built on this page; its de Rham version is on [[poincare-duality]].

blocks.title: Cochains on a simplicial complex
blocks.body:
After this section you can compute $H^0$, $H^1$ and $H^2$ of a small simplicial complex by hand from cochains, and read the cocycle conditions written in data-analysis and lattice papers.

Start with a question that has nothing to do with topology. Assign a number $\theta_{ij}$ to every edge $[i,j]$ ($i<j$) of a graph. When is there a function $f$ on the vertices with $\theta_{ij}=f(j)-f(i)$ for every edge, that is, when are the edge numbers differences of vertex values? Along any path the differences telescope, so a necessary condition is that $\theta$ sums to zero around every closed path, with signs according to the direction of travel. For the filled triangle with vertices $0,1,2$ the only closed path goes round the boundary, and the condition reads
$$\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}=\theta_{02}.$$
Imposing this on every triangle of a simplicial complex gives the cocycle condition $\theta^{ij}+\theta^{jk}=\theta^{ik}$ that Scoccola et al. write for $1$-cocycles before computing circular coordinates. For the hollow triangle there is no triangle to impose it on, and $\theta=(\theta_{01},\theta_{12},\theta_{02})=(1,0,0)$ is not a difference: the sum round the loop, $\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}-\theta_{02}=1$, is an obstruction. The first cohomology group will be exactly the group of such obstructions.

The general definition dualises the simplicial chain complex of [[homology]]: there a simplex $[v_0,\dots,v_n]$ with $v_0<\dots<v_n$ has boundary $\sum_i(-1)^i[v_0,\dots,\widehat{v_i},\dots,v_n]$.

blocks.title: Simplicial cochains and cohomology
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a simplicial complex with ordered vertices and $G$ an abelian group. The group of $n$-cochains is
$$C^n(K;G)=\mathrm{Hom}\big(C_n(K),G\big),$$
which is the same as the group of all functions from the set of $n$-simplices of $K$ to $G$ (a homomorphism on the free group $C_n(K)$ is determined by its values on the basis). The coboundary $\delta\colon C^n(K;G)\to C^{n+1}(K;G)$ is the dual of $\partial_{n+1}$:
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\partial\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^i\,\varphi\big([v_0,\dots,\widehat{v_i},\dots,v_{n+1}]\big)$$
for $\sigma=[v_0,\dots,v_{n+1}]$. Since $\partial\partial=0$, also $\delta\delta=0$. Cocycles are $Z^n=\ker\delta$, coboundaries are $B^n=\operatorname{im}\delta$, and the $n$-th cohomology group is
$$H^n(K;G)=Z^n/B^n.$$
In low degrees: $(\delta f)[v_0,v_1]=f(v_1)-f(v_0)$, and
$$\begin{aligned}(\delta\theta)[v_0,v_1,v_2]={}&\theta[v_1,v_2]-\theta[v_0,v_2]\\&+\theta[v_0,v_1]\end{aligned}.$$


For a simplex $\tau$ write $\tau^*$ for its indicator cochain ($1$ on $\tau$, $0$ on all other simplices). Then
$$\delta\tau^*=\sum_{\sigma\supset\tau}(-1)^{i(\sigma)}\,\sigma^*,$$
the sum over the $(n+1)$-simplices $\sigma$ having $\tau$ as a face, where $i(\sigma)$ is the position of the vertex of $\sigma$ not in $\tau$. With $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ the signs disappear and $\delta\tau^*$ is the sum of the cofaces of $\tau$; this is the form in which Chen and Tata write the coboundary on a lattice.

In words: an $n$-cochain is a function on $n$-simplices, and it is a cocycle when it is consistent on every $(n+1)$-simplex.

blocks.title: Cochains on the hollow and the filled triangle
blocks.body: Compute $H^0$, $H^1$ and $H^2$ with integer coefficients for the hollow triangle (vertices $0,1,2$ and the three edges) and for the filled triangle (add the $2$-simplex $[0,1,2]$). Find an explicit cocycle representing a generator of $H^1$ of the hollow triangle.
blocks.solution:
Order the edges as $[0,1],[0,2],[1,2]$ and identify a $1$-cochain $\theta$ with the column $(\theta_{01},\theta_{02},\theta_{12})$.

Degree $0$. A $0$-cochain $f=(f_0,f_1,f_2)$ has $\delta f=(f_1-f_0,\ f_2-f_0,\ f_2-f_1)$. So $\delta f=0$ exactly when $f$ is constant, and there are no coboundaries in degree $0$. Hence $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$ for both complexes.

Hollow triangle, degree $1$. There are no $2$-simplices, so every $1$-cochain is a cocycle: $Z^1=\mathbb{Z}^3$. The coboundaries are the cochains $(f_1-f_0,f_2-f_0,f_2-f_1)$. The homomorphism
$$\Phi(\theta)=\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}-\theta_{02}$$
(evaluation on the cycle $z=[0,1]+[1,2]-[0,2]$) vanishes on coboundaries, since $(f_1-f_0)+(f_2-f_1)-(f_2-f_0)=0$. Conversely, if $\Phi(\theta)=0$ put $f_0=0$, $f_1=\theta_{01}$, $f_2=\theta_{02}$; then $f_2-f_1=\theta_{02}-\theta_{01}=\theta_{12}$, so $\theta=\delta f$. Thus $B^1=\ker\Phi$ and $\Phi$ induces $H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}$ ($\Phi$ is onto, as $\Phi([0,1]^*)=1$). The cocycle $[0,1]^*$, which is $1$ on the edge $[0,1]$ and $0$ on the others, represents a generator; so do $[1,2]^*$ and $-[0,2]^*$, and they are cohomologous because their differences are coboundaries.

Filled triangle. Now $\delta\theta[0,1,2]=\theta_{12}-\theta_{02}+\theta_{01}=\Phi(\theta)$, so $Z^1=\ker\Phi=B^1$ and $H^1=0$. In degree $2$, $C^2=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\delta\colon C^1\to C^2$ is $\Phi$, which is onto, so $H^2=0$.

The matrices tell the same story: the matrix of $\delta_n$ is the transpose of the matrix of $\partial_{n+1}$, so $\delta$ and $\partial$ have the same rank, and the answers match the homology computed on [[homology]]: $\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}$ for the circle and $\mathbb{Z},0,0$ for the disc. The difference between the two theories shows up only in torsion, which moves up one degree; that is the universal coefficient theorem below.

items.q: On the hollow triangle, what is $\delta$ of the $0$-cochain $0^*$ that is $1$ on the vertex $0$ and $0$ on the vertices $1,2$?
Why is $H^0(K;G)$ the group of $G$-valued functions that are constant on each connected component?
items.a: $\delta f=0$ says $f(v_0)=f(v_1)$ for every edge, and there are no coboundaries in degree $0$ to divide by.

items.q: With $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients on the filled triangle, what is $\delta[0,1]^*$?
items.a: The sum of the cofaces of $[0,1]$, which is $[0,1,2]^*$ (with integer coefficients it is $+[0,1,2]^*$ too, since the missing vertex $2$ is in position $2$).

blocks.title: The boundary of a tetrahedron
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be the boundary of the tetrahedron on the vertices $0,1,2,3$ (four triangles, six edges, four vertices). Compute $H^2(K;\mathbb{Z})$ and show that it is detected by evaluation on the fundamental cycle
$$c=[1,2,3]-[0,2,3]+[0,1,3]-[0,1,2].$$
blocks.solution:
The cycle $c$ was found on [[homology]]: it spans $\ker\partial_2$. Define $\mathrm{ev}_c\colon C^2(K;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}^4\to\mathbb{Z}$ by $\mathrm{ev}_c(\omega)=\omega(c)$. For a $1$-cochain $\theta$, $\mathrm{ev}_c(\delta\theta)=\theta(\partial c)=0$, so $\mathrm{ev}_c$ kills coboundaries and induces a homomorphism $H^2\to\mathbb{Z}$, onto because $\mathrm{ev}_c([1,2,3]^*)=1$.

It remains to show $\ker\mathrm{ev}_c=B^2$. The matrix of $\delta_1$ is the transpose of the $6\times4$ matrix of $\partial_2$, whose rank is $3$; so $B^2$ is a rank-$3$ subgroup of the rank-$3$ group $\ker\mathrm{ev}_c$. To see equality (and not just finite index), take $\omega\in\ker\mathrm{ev}_c$ and try to write it as $\delta\theta$ with $\theta$ supported on the three edges $[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]$ at the vertex $0$. Writing $\theta_{0j}=\theta[0,j]$,
$$(\delta\theta)[0,1,2]=-\theta_{02}+\theta_{01},\quad(\delta\theta)[0,1,3]=-\theta_{03}+\theta_{01},\quad(\delta\theta)[0,2,3]=-\theta_{03}+\theta_{02},$$
and $(\delta\theta)[1,2,3]=0$. Every triangle except $[1,2,3]$ contains $0$. First replace $\omega$ by $\omega'=\omega-\omega[1,2,3]\,\delta([1,2]^*)$. Since $\delta[1,2]^*=[0,1,2]^*+[1,2,3]^*$ (the vertex not in $[1,2]$ sits in position $0$, respectively $2$, so both signs are $+$), $\omega'$ vanishes on $[1,2,3]$, and $\mathrm{ev}_c(\omega')=\mathrm{ev}_c(\omega)=0$. Now choose the integers $\theta_{01}=0$, $\theta_{02}=-\omega'[0,1,2]$, $\theta_{03}=-\omega'[0,1,3]$. Then $\delta\theta$ agrees with $\omega'$ on $[0,1,2]$, $[0,1,3]$ and $[1,2,3]$, and on $[0,2,3]$ it equals $\theta_{02}-\theta_{03}=\omega'[0,1,3]-\omega'[0,1,2]$, which is $\omega'[0,2,3]$ precisely because $\mathrm{ev}_c(\omega')=\omega'[1,2,3]-\omega'[0,2,3]+\omega'[0,1,3]-\omega'[0,1,2]=0$. So $\omega'=\delta\theta$ and $\omega$ is a coboundary. Hence $\ker\mathrm{ev}_c=B^2$ and
$$H^2(K;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z},\qquad[\omega]\mapsto\omega(c).$$
The class of any single triangle's indicator cochain, $[1,2,3]^*$ for instance, is a generator. The same pattern, a top class detected by evaluation on a fundamental cycle, reappears on every closed triangulated surface below.

blocks.title: What a cohomology class is
blocks.body: The definition is short; the sources read it in noticeably different ways, and each reading is used somewhere on this page.

items.label: Functions on simplices
items.body: A $k$-cochain is a function on the $k$-simplices, and the coboundary is the adjoint of the boundary under the pairing $\langle\varphi,c\rangle=\varphi(c)$. Chen and Tata use $\mathbb{Z}/2$ cochains on a triangulated lattice as field configurations, with $\delta$ of an indicator cochain the sum of its cofaces; Scoccola et al. use integer and real $1$-cocycles $\theta^{ij}$ on a complex built from data and turn them into circle-valued coordinates.

items.label: Local-to-global obstruction
items.body: The coboundary measures the failure of a compatibility condition, and a cohomology class is a compatible family modulo the trivially compatible ones. Nonzero classes are obstructions to making local data global, as the twist of the Möbius band is detected by a degree-one class on its core circle.

items.label: Functionals on homology
items.body: Evaluation of cochains on chains descends to the Kronecker pairing $H^n(X;M)\times H_n(X)\to M$, so each class gives a homomorphism $\kappa\colon H^n(X;M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(X),M)$. Quick leaves open whether $\kappa$ is injective or surjective and answers it with the universal coefficient theorem: it is onto, with kernel $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(X),M)$.

items.label: Maps to a classifying space
items.body: For a based CW complex $X$, reduced $H^n(X;G)$ is in natural bijection with based homotopy classes of maps $X\to K(G,n)$, a class being the pullback of a fundamental class. Cohomology classes are maps; for $n=1$, $G=\mathbb{Z}$ the target is the circle, a case proved below.

items.q: Compute $H^*(K;\mathbb{Z})$ for the graph $K$ with vertices $0,1,2,3$ and edges $[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[0,3],[0,2]$ (a square with one diagonal, no triangles), and give cocycles representing a basis of $H^1$.
items.hint: There are no $2$-simplices, so $Z^1=C^1$. Count: $H^1$ has rank equal to the number of independent loops.
items.solution: $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$ (connected). The coboundaries $\delta f$ form a subgroup of rank $4-1=3$ in $C^1=\mathbb{Z}^5$, and it is a direct summand: $\theta\mapsto(\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}-\theta_{02},\ \theta_{02}+\theta_{23}-\theta_{03})$ (evaluation on the two triangle-shaped loops $z_1=[0,1]+[1,2]-[0,2]$, $z_2=[0,2]+[2,3]-[0,3]$) maps $C^1$ onto $\mathbb{Z}^2$ with kernel exactly $B^1$ (if both sums vanish, integrate $\theta$ along the tree $[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]$ to get $f$ with $\delta f=\theta$). So $H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$, with basis the classes of $[1,2]^*$ (value $(1,0)$) and $[2,3]^*$ (value $(0,1)$). $H^n=0$ for $n\ge2$.

items.q: Show that the matrix of $\delta_n\colon C^n\to C^{n+1}$ in the bases of indicator cochains is the transpose of the matrix of $\partial_{n+1}$, and deduce that with coefficients in a field $F$, $\dim H^n(K;F)=\dim H_n(K;F)$ for a finite complex.
items.hint: The $(\sigma,\tau)$ entry of $\delta$ is $(\delta\tau^*)(\sigma)=\tau^*(\partial\sigma)$.
items.solution:
$(\delta\tau^*)(\sigma)=\tau^*(\partial\sigma)$ is the coefficient of $\tau$ in $\partial\sigma$, i.e. the $(\tau,\sigma)$ entry of $\partial_{n+1}$. Transposition preserves rank, so with $c_n$ the number of $n$-simplices,
$$\begin{aligned}\dim H^n&=(c_n-\operatorname{rank}\delta_n)-\operatorname{rank}\delta_{n-1}\\&=(c_n-\operatorname{rank}\partial_{n+1})-\operatorname{rank}\partial_n\end{aligned},$$
while $\dim H_n=(c_n-\operatorname{rank}\partial_n)-\operatorname{rank}\partial_{n+1}$. They are equal.

items.q: For the hollow square with vertices $0,1,2,3$ and edges $[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[0,3]$, decide which of the integer $1$-cochains $\theta=(\theta_{01},\theta_{12},\theta_{23},\theta_{03})$ equal to $(1,1,1,1)$, $(1,1,1,3)$ and $(2,0,0,-1)$ are coboundaries, and which pairs are cohomologous.
items.hint: The obstruction is the signed sum round the loop, $\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}+\theta_{23}-\theta_{03}$.
items.solution: As for the triangle, $\theta$ is a coboundary iff $\Phi(\theta)=\theta_{01}+\theta_{12}+\theta_{23}-\theta_{03}=0$, and $\Phi$ induces $H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}$. The values are $\Phi(1,1,1,1)=2$, $\Phi(1,1,1,3)=0$, $\Phi(2,0,0,-1)=3$. So only $(1,1,1,3)$ is a coboundary (it is $\delta f$ for $f=(0,1,2,3)$), and no two of the three are cohomologous since their values $2,0,3$ differ.

items.q: Let $K$ be any simplicial complex and $\theta$ a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-valued $1$-cocycle. Show that on every triangle $\theta$ takes the value $1$ on an even number of edges. Interpret: if $\theta$ is the indicator of the set of edges crossed by a curve drawn on a triangulated surface transversally to the edges, why is $\theta$ a cocycle when the curve is closed?
items.hint: Mod $2$, $(\delta\theta)[v_0,v_1,v_2]$ is the sum of the three edge values.
items.solution: Mod $2$ the signs vanish, so $\delta\theta=0$ on $[v_0,v_1,v_2]$ says $\theta[v_1,v_2]+\theta[v_0,v_2]+\theta[v_0,v_1]=0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/2$, i.e. an even number of the three values is $1$. A closed curve meeting a triangle transversally (and avoiding vertices) enters and leaves it the same number of times, so it crosses its boundary an even number of times; parity of crossings per edge then satisfies the condition. This is Hatcher's picture of degree-one cocycles on surfaces as counting crossings with a transverse curve.

items.q:
Show that for a finite simplicial complex $K$ and the coefficient field $\mathbb{Q}$, the composite
$$Z^n(K;\mathbb{Q})\to H^n(K;\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(K;\mathbb{Q}),\mathbb{Q}),$$
$[\varphi]\mapsto([z]\mapsto\varphi(z))$, is a well-defined isomorphism.
items.hint: Well defined: cocycles vanish on boundaries, coboundaries vanish on cycles. For bijectivity use linear algebra: choose a complement of $B_n$ in $Z_n$ and of $Z_n$ in $C_n$.
items.solution: If $\delta\varphi=0$ and $z=\partial w$ then $\varphi(z)=\delta\varphi(w)=0$; if $\varphi=\delta\eta$ and $\partial z=0$ then $\varphi(z)=\eta(\partial z)=0$. So the map is well defined. Injective: suppose $\varphi$ is a cocycle vanishing on $Z_n$. Then $\varphi$ factors through $C_n/Z_n\cong B_{n-1}$ via $\partial$: $\varphi=\psi\circ\partial$ with $\psi$ linear on $B_{n-1}$; extend $\psi$ to $C_{n-1}$ (vector spaces), so $\varphi=\delta\psi$. Surjective: a linear map $\lambda$ on $Z_n/B_n$ is a linear map on $Z_n$ vanishing on $B_n$; extend it to $\varphi$ on $C_n$ using a complement of $Z_n$. Then $\delta\varphi(w)=\varphi(\partial w)=0$ as $\partial w\in B_n$, so $\varphi$ is a cocycle mapping to $\lambda$.

blocks.body:
- $C^n(K;G)=\mathrm{Hom}(C_n(K),G)$ = functions on $n$-simplices; $(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\partial\sigma)$, $\delta\delta=0$, $H^n=\ker\delta/\operatorname{im}\delta$.
- $H^0$ = locally constant functions; a $1$-cochain is a coboundary iff its signed sums round all closed edge paths vanish.
- The matrix of $\delta_n$ is the transpose of that of $\partial_{n+1}$; ranks, hence field Betti numbers, agree with homology.
- Top classes of a triangulated sphere or surface are detected by evaluation on the fundamental cycle.

blocks.title: Singular cohomology and its basic properties
blocks.body:
After this section you can compute cohomology with the long exact sequence of a pair, excision and Mayer–Vietoris, and you know why each of these follows from its homology counterpart.

Simplicial cochains depend on a triangulation. As for homology, the remedy is to use all singular simplices. Every property below is obtained by applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,G)$ to a chain-level statement about singular chains; the only care needed is that $\mathrm{Hom}(-,G)$ is not exact in general (see [[homological-algebra]]), so one must check that the sequences being dualised split.

blocks.title: Singular cochains and cohomology
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a space and $G$ an abelian group. Let $C_n(X)$ be the singular chain group of [[homology]], free on the continuous maps $\sigma\colon\Delta^n\to X$. The singular $n$-cochains are
$$C^n(X;G)=\mathrm{Hom}\big(C_n(X),G\big)=\{\text{functions }\{\sigma\colon\Delta^n\to X\}\to G\},$$
with coboundary $(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\partial\sigma)$, and $H^n(X;G)=\ker\delta_n/\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}$. For $A\subseteq X$, the relative cochains are those vanishing on chains in $A$,
$$C^n(X,A;G)=\ker\big(C^n(X;G)\to C^n(A;G)\big)=\mathrm{Hom}\big(C_n(X)/C_n(A),G\big),$$
and $H^n(X,A;G)$ is the cohomology of this subcomplex. When $G=R$ is a ring we write $H^n(X;R)$, and $H^*(X;R)=\bigoplus_nH^n(X;R)$.

Evaluation $\langle\varphi,c\rangle=\varphi(c)$ satisfies $\langle\delta\varphi,c\rangle=\langle\varphi,\partial c\rangle$, so it descends to the Kronecker pairing $H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X)\to G$ and to a homomorphism $\kappa\colon H^n(X;G)\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(X),G)$.

blocks.title: A point, and degree zero
blocks.body: Compute $H^*(\mathrm{pt};G)$, and show that $H^0(X;G)$ is the group of all functions $\pi_0(X)\to G$ from the set of path components.
blocks.solution:
For a point there is exactly one singular $n$-simplex $c_n$ in each degree, so $C^n(\mathrm{pt};G)\cong G$. Its boundary is $\partial c_n=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^ic_{n-1}$, which is $c_{n-1}$ for $n$ even and $n\ge2$ and $0$ for $n$ odd. Dually, $\delta_{n-1}\colon C^{n-1}\to C^n$ is multiplication by $1$ for $n$ even and $n\ge2$, and $0$ for $n$ odd. The cochain complex is
$$G\xrightarrow{0}G\xrightarrow{1}G\xrightarrow{0}G\xrightarrow{1}\cdots,$$
so $H^0=G$ and $H^n=0$ for $n\ge1$: in degree $n\ge1$ odd the kernel is $0$ (the outgoing map is $1$), and in degree $n\ge2$ even the kernel is everything and the image is everything.

Degree zero. A $0$-cochain is an arbitrary function $f\colon X\to G$ (one value for each point, no continuity). For a path $\sigma\colon\Delta^1\to X$, $(\delta f)(\sigma)=f(\sigma(1))-f(\sigma(0))$. So $f$ is a cocycle iff it is constant along paths, i.e. constant on path components. There are no coboundaries in degree $0$, so $H^0(X;G)=\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0(X),G)$. For infinitely many components this is a product, not a direct sum: $H^0$ of a countable discrete space is $G^{\mathbb{N}}$, while $H_0$ is $\bigoplus_{\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Z}$.

Miller adds a warning that is worth keeping: $C^n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is a product of copies of $\mathbb{Z}$ over the usually uncountable set of singular simplices, and it is never a free abelian group (unless it is zero). Statements proved for free chain complexes do not apply to cochain complexes automatically.

blocks.title: Basic properties of singular cohomology
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be an abelian group.

1. Functoriality. A map $f\colon X\to Y$ induces $f^*\colon H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$, $(f^*\varphi)(\sigma)=\varphi(f\circ\sigma)$, with $(gf)^*=f^*g^*$ and $\mathrm{id}^*=\mathrm{id}$; similarly for maps of pairs.
2. Homotopy invariance. Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism; homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic cohomology.
3. Long exact sequence of a pair. For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}\cdots&\to H^n(X,A;G)\to H^n(X;G)\to H^n(A;G)\\&\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }H^{n+1}(X,A;G)\to H^{n+1}(X;G)\to\cdots\end{aligned}$$
where $\delta[\varphi]=[\delta\tilde\varphi]$ for any cochain $\tilde\varphi$ on $X$ extending the cocycle $\varphi$ on $A$.
4. Excision. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and the closure of $Z$ lies in the interior of $A$, then restriction $H^n(X,A;G)\to H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$ is an isomorphism for all $n$.
5. Mayer–Vietoris. If $X$ is the union of the interiors of $A$ and $B$, there is an exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}\cdots&\to H^n(X)\to H^n(A)\oplus H^n(B)\to H^n(A\cap B)\\&\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots\end{aligned}$$
with maps $\varphi\mapsto(\varphi|_A,\varphi|_B)$ and $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha|_{A\cap B}-\beta|_{A\cap B}$.
6. Disjoint unions. For $X=\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ the inclusions induce $H^n(X;G)\cong\prod_\alpha H^n(X_\alpha;G)$.
7. Reduced cohomology. For $X\neq\varnothing$ and $x_0\in X$ put $\tilde H^n(X;G)=H^n(X,x_0;G)$; then $H^n=\tilde H^n$ for $n>0$ and $H^0(X;G)\cong\tilde H^0(X;G)\oplus G$. Mayer–Vietoris holds for $\tilde H$ when $A\cap B\neq\varnothing$.

Idea: dualise the corresponding chain-level facts. Two algebraic lemmas make dualising safe.

Lemma 1 (Quick, Lecture 18). If $0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$ is an exact sequence of chain complexes of free abelian groups, then
$$\begin{aligned}0\to\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet,G)&\to\mathrm{Hom}(B_\bullet,G)\\&\to\mathrm{Hom}(A_\bullet,G)\to0\end{aligned}$$
is exact. Proof: $C_n$ is free, so each $0\to A_n\to B_n\to C_n\to0$ splits, and $\mathrm{Hom}(-,G)$ is additive, so it carries split exact sequences to split exact sequences.

Lemma 2. If a chain map $u\colon C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ of complexes of free abelian groups induces isomorphisms on all homology groups, then $u^*\colon H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(D_\bullet,G))\to H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet,G))$ is an isomorphism for all $n$. Proof: the universal coefficient sequence of [[ext]] (stated in the next section) is natural, so $u$ gives a map between the sequences
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1},G)\to H^n\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n,G)\to0$$
for $D$ and for $C$. The outer maps are induced by the isomorphisms $u_*$ on homology, so they are isomorphisms, and the five lemma (on the short sequences padded with zeros) shows the middle map is one.

Now the properties.

1. $f^*$ commutes with $\delta$ because $f_\sharp\colon C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet(Y)$ commutes with $\partial$; functoriality is that of $f_\sharp$.

2. If $f\simeq g$, the homology proof gives a chain homotopy $h$ with $g_\sharp-f_\sharp=\partial h+h\partial$. Apply $\mathrm{Hom}(-,G)$: $g^\sharp-f^\sharp=h^*\delta+\delta h^*$, where $h^*\varphi=\varphi\circ h$. A cocycle $\varphi$ therefore satisfies $g^\sharp\varphi-f^\sharp\varphi=\delta(h^*\varphi)$, so $f^*=g^*$ on cohomology.

3. $C_n(A)\subseteq C_n(X)$ is spanned by a subset of the basis, so $C_n(X)/C_n(A)$ is free on the simplices not in $A$. Lemma 1 applied to $0\to C_\bullet(A)\to C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet(X)/C_\bullet(A)\to0$ gives the short exact sequence $0\to C^\bullet(X,A)\to C^\bullet(X)\to C^\bullet(A)\to0$; concretely, restriction is onto because a cochain on $A$ extends by zero. The long exact sequence of [[homological-algebra]] is the claimed sequence, and the recipe for its connecting map (lift, apply $\delta$, pull back) is the formula $\delta[\varphi]=[\delta\tilde\varphi]$.

4. Excision for homology is proved by showing that the inclusion $C_\bullet(X\setminus Z)/C_\bullet(A\setminus Z)\to C_\bullet(X)/C_\bullet(A)$ induces isomorphisms on homology (by subdividing chains into small simplices; Quick follows the homology case, Hatcher Ch. 2). Both complexes are free, so Lemma 2 gives the cohomology statement.

5. Let $C_\bullet(A+B)\subseteq C_\bullet(X)$ be the chains that are sums of chains in $A$ and chains in $B$. The small-chains theorem behind homology Mayer–Vietoris says the inclusion $C_\bullet(A+B)\to C_\bullet(X)$ induces isomorphisms on homology. The sequence
$$0\to C_\bullet(A\cap B)\xrightarrow{\ c\mapsto(c,-c)\ }C_\bullet(A)\oplus C_\bullet(B)\xrightarrow{\ (a,b)\mapsto a+b\ }C_\bullet(A+B)\to0$$
is exact and consists of free groups ($C_n(A+B)$ is free on the simplices lying in $A$ or in $B$). By Lemma 1 its dual is exact, its long exact sequence is a Mayer–Vietoris sequence with $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(A+B),G))$ in place of $H^n(X;G)$, and Lemma 2 identifies the two. Dualising the maps gives restriction to $(A,B)$ and the difference $\alpha-\beta$ on $A\cap B$.

6. $C_n(\bigsqcup X_\alpha)=\bigoplus C_n(X_\alpha)$ because a simplex has path-connected image, and $\mathrm{Hom}(\bigoplus_\alpha-,G)=\prod_\alpha\mathrm{Hom}(-,G)$; products of cochain complexes have the product of the cohomologies.

7. The pair $(X,x_0)$ has the long exact sequence of 3. The map $H^n(X)\to H^n(x_0)$ is split onto by the constant map $X\to x_0$, and $H^n(x_0)=0$ for $n>0$, so the long sequence breaks into $0\to\tilde H^n(X)\to H^n(X)\to H^n(x_0)\to0$, split. The reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence follows by comparing the sequences for $X$ and for a point, as in homology.

blocks.title: Spheres, discs and relative classes
blocks.body:
(a) Compute $\tilde H^n(S^k;G)$ for $k\ge1$ by Mayer–Vietoris, without using homology.

(b) Compute $H^n(D^k,S^{k-1};G)$ and describe a generator of $H^1([0,1],\{0,1\};\mathbb{Z})$ by a cochain.
blocks.solution:
(a) Let $A=S^k\setminus\{\text{south pole}\}$ and $B=S^k\setminus\{\text{north pole}\}$. Both are homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^k$, hence contractible, so $\tilde H^*(A)=\tilde H^*(B)=0$ by homotopy invariance and the computation for a point; $A\cap B$ deformation retracts onto the equator $S^{k-1}$. The reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence contains
$$\tilde H^{n-1}(A)\oplus\tilde H^{n-1}(B)\to\tilde H^{n-1}(A\cap B)\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }\tilde H^n(S^k)\to\tilde H^n(A)\oplus\tilde H^n(B),$$
whose outer terms vanish. So $\tilde H^n(S^k)\cong\tilde H^{n-1}(S^{k-1})$, and by induction $\tilde H^n(S^k)\cong\tilde H^{n-k}(S^0)$. For $S^0=\{p,q\}$, $H^0=G\times G$ and $\tilde H^0(S^0)=H^0(S^0,q)\cong G$ (functions on $\{p,q\}$ vanishing at $q$), with nothing in higher degrees. Hence $\tilde H^n(S^k;G)\cong G$ for $n=k$ and $0$ otherwise.

(b) In the long exact sequence of $(D^k,S^{k-1})$ the groups $\tilde H^*(D^k)$ vanish ($D^k$ is contractible; use the reduced form of the sequence, which is exact for the same reason). So $\delta\colon\tilde H^{n-1}(S^{k-1})\to H^n(D^k,S^{k-1})$ is an isomorphism, and $H^n(D^k,S^{k-1};G)\cong G$ for $n=k$ and $0$ otherwise.

For $k=1$: $\tilde H^0(\{0,1\};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ is generated by the function $g$ that is $1$ at the point $1$ and $0$ at the point $0$. By the recipe for $\delta$, extend $g$ to a $0$-cochain $\tilde g$ on $[0,1]$ (say $\tilde g(x)=1$ for $x=1$ and $0$ otherwise) and take $\delta\tilde g$. On the path $\sigma(t)=t$ it gives $\tilde g(1)-\tilde g(0)=1$, and it vanishes on the constant simplices at the endpoints, so $\delta\tilde g$ is a relative $1$-cocycle. Its class generates $H^1([0,1],\{0,1\};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, and evaluating it on the relative cycle $\sigma$ gives $1$. This is the cohomological shadow of the fundamental theorem of calculus: the relative class integrates to the difference of boundary values.

items.q: Why is restriction $C^n(X;G)\to C^n(A;G)$ surjective, while the corresponding map $H^n(X;G)\to H^n(A;G)$ need not be?
items.a: A cochain on $A$ is a function on simplices in $A$ and extends by $0$; but an extension of a cocycle need not be a cocycle. Example: $H^0([0,1];G)=G\to H^0(\{0,1\};G)=G^2$ is not onto.

items.q: In which direction does the connecting map of the Mayer–Vietoris sequence go in cohomology?
items.a: Up in degree: $H^n(A\cap B)\to H^{n+1}(X)$, the reverse of homology's $H_{n+1}(X)\to H_n(A\cap B)$.

items.q: What does property 6 give for a countable disjoint union of points, and how does it differ from homology?
items.a: $H^0=\prod_{\mathbb{N}}G$, a product; homology gives the direct sum $\bigoplus_{\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $0$.

items.q: Compute $H^*(S^1\vee S^1;\mathbb{Z})$ using Mayer–Vietoris.
items.hint: Take $A$ and $B$ to be each circle together with a small open arc of the other circle around the wedge point.
items.solution:
$A\simeq S^1$, $B\simeq S^1$, $A\cap B$ is a contractible cross around the wedge point, and $A\cup B=S^1\vee S^1$. The reduced sequence
$$\begin{aligned}\tilde H^{n-1}(A\cap B)&\to\tilde H^n(X)\\&\to\tilde H^n(A)\oplus\tilde H^n(B)\to\tilde H^n(A\cap B)\end{aligned}$$
has $\tilde H^*(A\cap B)=0$, so $\tilde H^n(X)\cong\tilde H^n(S^1)\oplus\tilde H^n(S^1)$: $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$, $H^1=\mathbb{Z}^2$, $H^n=0$ for $n\ge2$.

items.q: Show that $H^n(X,X;G)=0$ for all $n$ and that $H^n(X,\varnothing;G)=H^n(X;G)$, and check that the long exact sequence of the pair $(X,X)$ is consistent with this.
items.hint: Look at the cochain groups.
items.solution: $C^n(X,X)$ consists of cochains vanishing on all simplices of $X$, so it is $0$; $C^n(X,\varnothing)=C^n(X)$ since the condition is empty. In the sequence for $(X,X)$ the maps $H^n(X)\to H^n(X)$ are identities and the relative groups are $0$, which is exact.

items.q: Compute $H^*(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p,q\};\mathbb{Z})$ for two distinct points $p,q$.
items.hint: Cover by two open half-planes, each containing one puncture, overlapping in a strip.
items.solution: Let $A$, $B$ be the open half-planes $\{x<\varepsilon\}$ and $\{x>-\varepsilon\}$ with $p=(-1,0)\in A$, $q=(1,0)\in B$. Then $A\setminus\{p\}\simeq S^1$, $B\setminus\{q\}\simeq S^1$, and their intersection is the strip $\{|x|<\varepsilon\}$, contractible. As in the previous exercise $\tilde H^n(X)\cong\tilde H^n(S^1)^2$: $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$, $H^1=\mathbb{Z}^2$, $H^2=0$. (The [[de-rham-cohomology]] page finds the same answer over $\mathbb{R}$ with angle forms.)

items.q: Let $A\subseteq X$ be a retract, with retraction $r\colon X\to A$. Show that $H^n(X;G)\cong H^n(A;G)\oplus H^n(X,A;G)$.
items.hint: Restriction $i^*$ has the right inverse $r^*$; use exactness.
items.solution: $ri=\mathrm{id}_A$ gives $i^*r^*=\mathrm{id}$, so $i^*\colon H^n(X)\to H^n(A)$ is onto for every $n$. Then the connecting maps $\delta\colon H^n(A)\to H^{n+1}(X,A)$ are zero, so the long exact sequence breaks into short exact sequences $0\to H^n(X,A)\to H^n(X)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^n(A)\to0$, split by $r^*$; hence $H^n(X)\cong H^n(A)\oplus H^n(X,A)$.

items.q: Prove the five lemma step used in Lemma 2 of the proof directly: if $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ and $0\to A'\to B'\to C'\to0$ are exact and $\beta\colon B\to B'$ restricts and descends to isomorphisms $A\to A'$, $C\to C'$, then $\beta$ is an isomorphism. Then explain why naturality of the universal coefficient sequence, not just its existence, is needed in Lemma 2.
items.hint: Diagram chase; without naturality there is no map between the two sequences to chase in.
items.solution: Injective: if $\beta(b)=0$, its image in $C'$ is $0$, so the image of $b$ in $C$ is $0$ and $b$ comes from $a\in A$; then the image of $a$ in $A'$ maps to $\beta(b)=0$ in $B'$, and $A'\to B'$ is injective, so $a\mapsto0$ in $A'$, hence $a=0$ and $b=0$. Surjective: for $b'\in B'$, take its image in $C'$, lift it to $C$ and then to $b\in B$; $b'-\beta(b)$ maps to $0$ in $C'$, so it comes from $a'\in A'$, which comes from $a\in A$; then $b'=\beta(b+a)$. Naturality is what provides $\beta$ as the map induced by $u$ on cohomology and makes the squares commute; abstract isomorphisms of the outer terms alone would give only an abstract isomorphism of the middle groups (which in fact also holds, by the non-natural splitting), not that $u^*$ is an isomorphism.

blocks.body:
- Singular cochains are functions on singular simplices; $H^*(X;G)$ is contravariant and homotopy invariant.
- Long exact sequence of a pair, excision, Mayer–Vietoris (connecting map raises degree), disjoint unions to products: each is a chain-level fact dualised.
- Dualising is safe because the chain sequences involved split (free groups), and homology isomorphisms of free complexes give cohomology isomorphisms.
- $\tilde H^n(S^k;G)=G$ for $n=k$, $0$ otherwise; $H^k(D^k,S^{k-1};G)=G$.

blocks.title: Universal coefficients: cohomology from homology
blocks.body:
After this section you can compute $H^n(X;G)$ for any coefficient group from the integral homology of $X$, tell which classes survive when coefficients change, and compute cohomology of CW complexes from their cells.

Computing cochains on all singular simplices is hopeless, and even simplicial cochains get large. Since $C_\bullet(X)$ is a complex of free abelian groups, the question 'how does $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet,G))$ depend on $H_\bullet(C)$?' is purely algebraic. The [[ext]] page answers it, as the universal coefficient theorem, for every chain complex of free abelian groups; here is what it says for spaces.

blocks.title: Universal coefficient theorem for cohomology
blocks.body:
For every space $X$ (or pair $(X,A)$), every abelian group $G$ and every $n$ there is a natural short exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}0\to\mathrm{Ext}\big(H_{n-1}(X),G\big)&\to H^n(X;G)\\&\xrightarrow{\ \kappa\ }\mathrm{Hom}\big(H_n(X),G\big)\to0,\end{aligned}$$
where $\kappa$ is the Kronecker map. It splits, but the splitting is not natural. Consequently:

1. If $H_n(X)\cong\mathbb{Z}^{b_n}\oplus T_n$ with $T_n$ finite for all $n$, then $H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{b_n}\oplus T_{n-1}$: the free part stays and the torsion moves up one degree.
2. $H^1(X;G)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(X),G)$, since $H_0(X)$ is free; for path-connected $X$ this is $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X),G)$ by Hurewicz.
3. If $F$ is a field, $H^n(X;F)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_F\big(H_n(X;F),F\big)$; for $F=\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$ also $H^n(X;F)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(X),F)$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}H^n(X;\mathbb{Q})=b_n$.

The exact sequence and its non-natural splitting are the universal coefficient theorem proved on [[ext]] for any complex of free abelian groups, applied to $C_\bullet(X)$ or to the free complex $C_\bullet(X)/C_\bullet(A)$.

1. $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^{b}\oplus T,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}^b$ because $\mathrm{Hom}(T,\mathbb{Z})=0$ for finite $T$; $\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}^b\oplus T,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathrm{Ext}(T,\mathbb{Z})\cong T$ by the computations on [[ext]] ($\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},-)=0$ and $\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/m$). The sequence splits.

2. $\mathrm{Ext}(H_0(X),G)=0$ because $H_0(X)$ is free.

3. Over a field (or any principal ideal domain) the proof on [[ext]] goes through word for word for complexes of free $F$-modules. Apply it to $C_\bullet(X;F)=C_\bullet(X)\otimes F$, which is free over $F$ and satisfies $\mathrm{Hom}_F(C_n(X)\otimes F,F)=\mathrm{Hom}(C_n(X),F)$. Over a field every module is projective, so $\mathrm{Ext}_F=0$ and $H^n(X;F)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_F(H_n(X;F),F)$. For $F=\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$, the group $F$ is divisible, hence injective as an abelian group, so $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(X),F)=0$ in the integral sequence as well.

blocks.title: Real projective spaces from their cells
blocks.body:
$\mathbb{RP}^n$ is a CW complex with one cell in each dimension $0,\dots,n$, and its cellular chain complex (Wikipedia, Cellular homology; Hatcher Ch. 2) is
$$0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{d_n}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_3}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{d_2}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{d_1}\mathbb{Z}\to0,\qquad d_k=1+(-1)^k,$$
so $d_k=2$ for $k$ even and $d_k=0$ for $k$ odd. Compute $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^n;G)$ for $G=\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Q}$, and write out $n=4,5$.
blocks.solution:
Homology. In degree $k$ with $0<k<n$: the incoming map $d_{k+1}$ is $2$ if $k$ is odd and $0$ if $k$ is even, the outgoing map $d_k$ is $0$ if $k$ is odd and $2$ (injective) if $k$ is even. So $H_k=\mathbb{Z}/2$ for odd $k<n$ and $H_k=0$ for even $0<k<n$. Also $H_0=\mathbb{Z}$, and $H_n=\ker d_n$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ for $n$ odd and $0$ for $n$ even. (Cellular homology computes singular homology for CW complexes.)

Integral cohomology, by consequence 1 (torsion moves up): $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$; for $0<k\le n$, $H^k=\mathbb{Z}/2$ if $k$ is even (from $T_{k-1}=\mathbb{Z}/2$), $H^k=0$ if $k$ is odd and $k<n$; and $H^n=\mathbb{Z}$ if $n$ is odd. For example
$$H^*(\mathbb{RP}^4;\mathbb{Z}):\ \mathbb{Z},0,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z}/2,\qquad H^*(\mathbb{RP}^5;\mathbb{Z}):\ \mathbb{Z},0,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}.$$

Mod $2$. Tensoring the cellular complex with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ makes all $d_k=0$, so $H_k(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $0\le k\le n$ and, by consequence 3, $H^k(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $0\le k\le n$. (Check with the integral sequence: $H^k=\mathrm{Hom}(H_k,\mathbb{Z}/2)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(H_{k-1},\mathbb{Z}/2)$, and exactly one of the two terms is $\mathbb{Z}/2$ for each $0<k<n$.)

Rationally, $H^k(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Q})=\mathrm{Hom}(H_k,\mathbb{Q})$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ for $k=0$, and for $k=n$ when $n$ is odd, and $0$ otherwise: $\mathbb{RP}^{2m}$ has the rational cohomology of a point and $\mathbb{RP}^{2m+1}$ that of $S^{2m+1}$.

blocks.title: Cellular cohomology
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a CW complex with cellular chain complex $C^{\mathrm{cell}}_n(X)=H_n(X^n,X^{n-1})$, free on the $n$-cells, with boundary given by the degrees of the attaching maps. Then
$$H^n(X;G)\cong H^n\big(\mathrm{Hom}(C^{\mathrm{cell}}_\bullet(X),G)\big)$$
for all $n$. If $A\subseteq X$ is a subcomplex, restriction $H^n(X;G)\to H^n(A;G)$ corresponds to restricting cellular cochains to the cells of $A$. In particular, if all cellular coboundaries vanish, $H^n(X;G)$ is the group of functions on the $n$-cells, and restriction to a subcomplex is the projection onto the cells of $A$.

The isomorphism of groups: both $C_\bullet(X)$ and $C^{\mathrm{cell}}_\bullet(X)$ are complexes of free abelian groups, and their homology groups are isomorphic by the theorem that cellular homology computes singular homology (Hatcher Ch. 2; Wikipedia, Cellular homology). The universal coefficient theorem expresses the cohomology of each of them by the same formula $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n,G)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1},G)$, so the groups are isomorphic. That the isomorphism can be chosen natural, compatible with restriction to subcomplexes, is proved in Hatcher §3.1 by running the cellular construction directly on cochains (the pairs $(X^n,X^{n-1})$ and their long exact sequences); we use the naturality only for projective spaces, where it is also stated in Hatcher §3.2.

blocks.title: Changing coefficients: what survives
blocks.body:
Let $X_m=S^1\cup_me^2$ be the circle with a $2$-cell attached by the map $z\mapsto z^m$ ($m\ge2$), so that $X_2=\mathbb{RP}^2$; its cellular complex is $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$.

(a) Compute $H^*(X_m;\mathbb{Z})$, $H^*(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)$ and $H^*(X_m;\mathbb{Q})$.

(b) Decide whether the reduction map $H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)$ is onto, and whether the image of $H^1(T^2;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(T^2;\mathbb{R})$ is a lattice.
blocks.solution:
(a) Homology: $H_0=\mathbb{Z}$, $H_1=\mathbb{Z}/m$, and $H_2=\ker d_2=0$ because $d_2$ is multiplication by $m$, which is injective. Integral cohomology by the universal coefficient theorem: $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$, $H^1=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z})=0$, $H^2=\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/m$. Directly from cellular cochains: $\mathrm{Hom}$ of the complex is $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb{Z}$, with the same answer. With $\mathbb{Z}/m$ coefficients the cochain complex is $\mathbb{Z}/m\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/m\xrightarrow{m=0}\mathbb{Z}/m$, so $H^k(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)=\mathbb{Z}/m$ for $k=0,1,2$. Rationally, $\mathbb{Q}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Q}\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb{Q}$ gives $H^0=\mathbb{Q}$ and $H^1=H^2=0$: rationally $X_m$ is a point.

(b) $H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z})=0$ while $H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)=\mathbb{Z}/m$, so reduction is not onto: a mod $m$ class need not come from an integral one. (The obstruction is measured by the Bockstein homomorphism, a topic for the page on cohomology operations.)

For the torus, $H_1(T^2)=\mathbb{Z}^2$ is free, so $H^1(T^2;\mathbb{Z})=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^1(T^2;\mathbb{R})=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{R})$, and the map is induced by $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$. Its image is $\mathbb{Z}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, a full lattice: a real class is integral exactly when its values on the two basic loops are integers. In general the image of $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(X;\mathbb{R})$ is the lattice $\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(X),\mathbb{Z})$ inside $\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(X),\mathbb{R})$, and torsion of $H^2$ dies; Scoccola et al. use exactly this lattice $H^1(B;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(B;\mathbb{R})$ to choose integral classes for circular coordinates by lattice reduction. Integral classes of de Rham cohomology are treated on [[de-rham-cohomology]].

blocks.body:
- $H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is not $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(X),\mathbb{Z})$ in general. For $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $\mathrm{Hom}(H_2,\mathbb{Z})=0$ but $H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/2$, coming from the torsion of $H_1$.
- The splitting of the universal coefficient sequence is not natural. A map $f$ can act as zero on $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n,G)$ and on $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1},G)$ and still be nonzero on $H^n$; one may not compute $f^*$ summand by summand.
- Over $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$ cohomology forgets torsion entirely; over $\mathbb{Z}/p$ it sees $p$-torsion twice, in $\mathrm{Hom}$ and in $\mathrm{Ext}$. The Klein bottle has mod $2$ Betti numbers $1,2,1$ like the torus (computed on [[ext]]) but rational ones $1,1,0$.
- A class with $\mathbb{Z}/m$ coefficients need not lift to $\mathbb{Z}$ ($X_m$ above), and an integral class can vanish over $\mathbb{Q}$ without vanishing ($H^2(X_m;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/m$).

items.q: Compute $H^*(S^1\vee\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^*(S^1\vee\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
items.hint: Reduced cohomology of a wedge of CW complexes is the product (here direct sum) of the reduced cohomologies, by Mayer–Vietoris.
items.solution: $\tilde H^*(S^1;\mathbb{Z})$: $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $1$. $\tilde H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$: $0,\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $1,2$. So $H^*(S^1\vee\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $0,1,2$. Mod $2$: $\tilde H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $1,2$, so $H^*=\mathbb{Z}/2,(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2,\mathbb{Z}/2$.

items.q: Show that $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free for every space $X$, and that $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})=0$ whenever $\pi_1(X)$ is finite ($X$ path connected).
items.hint: Consequence 2.
items.solution: $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(X),\mathbb{Z})$, and if $n\lambda=0$ for a homomorphism $\lambda$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ with $n\ne0$ then $\lambda=0$, since $\mathbb{Z}$ is torsion-free. If $\pi_1$ is finite, so is $H_1=\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}$, and every homomorphism from a finite group to $\mathbb{Z}$ is zero.

items.q: Let $X$ have finitely generated homology, $H_n(X)\cong\mathbb{Z}^{b_n}\oplus T_n$, and let $p$ be a prime. Show that $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H^n(X;\mathbb{Z}/p)=b_n+\tau_n+\tau_{n-1}$, where $\tau_k$ is the number of cyclic summands of $T_k$ of order divisible by $p$ (in a decomposition into cyclic groups of prime power order). Apply it to $\mathbb{RP}^5$ with $p=2$ and $p=3$.
items.hint: $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/q,\mathbb{Z}/p)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/q,\mathbb{Z}/p)$ are both $\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(q,p)$.
items.solution:
By the universal coefficient theorem
$$H^n(X;\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_n,\mathbb{Z}/p)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1},\mathbb{Z}/p).$$
$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/p)=\mathbb{Z}/p$, $\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},-)=0$, and for a cyclic summand $\mathbb{Z}/q$,
$$\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/q,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/q,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(q,p),$$
which is $\mathbb{Z}/p$ if $p\mid q$ and $0$ otherwise (see [[ext]]). Summing gives $b_n+\tau_n$ from Hom and $\tau_{n-1}$ from Ext. For $\mathbb{RP}^5$: $H_*=\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z}$. With $p=2$:
$$\begin{gathered}1+0+0,\ \ 0+1+0,\ \ 0+0+1,\\ 0+1+0,\ \ 0+0+1,\ \ 1+0+0\end{gathered},$$
i.e. $1$ in each degree $0,\dots,5$. With $p=3$: $\tau=0$ throughout, so $\dim H^k=b_k$: $1,0,0,0,0,1$.

items.q: Let $L$ be a connected CW complex with $H_1(L)\cong\mathbb{Z}/5$, $H_2(L)=0$ and $H_3(L)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, $H_n(L)=0$ for $n>3$ (for example a lens space). Compute $H^*(L;\mathbb{Z})$, $H^*(L;\mathbb{Z}/5)$ and $H^*(L;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
items.hint: Torsion moves up one degree; use the previous exercise for $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
items.solution: Integral: $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$, $H^1=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/5,\mathbb{Z})=0$, $H^2=\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/5,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/5$, $H^3=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$. Mod $5$: dimensions $1,\ 0+1,\ 0+1,\ 1$, so $\mathbb{Z}/5$ in each degree $0,1,2,3$. Mod $2$: $5$-torsion is invisible, dimensions $1,0,0,1$.

items.q: Give an example showing that the splitting in the universal coefficient theorem is not natural: find a map $f\colon X\to Y$ inducing $0$ on $\mathrm{Hom}(H_2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and on $\mathrm{Ext}(H_1,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ but a nonzero map $H^2(Y;\mathbb{Z}/2)\to H^2(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
items.hint: Take $X=\mathbb{RP}^2$, $Y=\mathbb{RP}^2/\mathbb{RP}^1\cong S^2$ and $f$ the quotient map; compute both sides with cellular cochains.
items.solution: Let $f\colon\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{RP}^2/\mathbb{RP}^1=S^2$ collapse the $1$-skeleton. On $H_2$: $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$, so the induced map on $\mathrm{Hom}(H_2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is $0$. On $H_1$: $H_1(S^2)=0$, so the map on $\mathrm{Ext}(H_1,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is $0$ as well. But $f$ is cellular and maps the $2$-cell of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ homeomorphically onto the $2$-cell of $S^2$ (it is the characteristic map of the top cell followed by the collapse), so on cellular cochains with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients it sends the generator of $C^2(S^2)$ to the generator of $C^2(\mathbb{RP}^2)$; all mod $2$ coboundaries vanish in both complexes, so $f^*\colon H^2(S^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)\to H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is an isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2$. In $H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ the class lies in the Ext part and in $H^2(S^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ in the Hom part, so no choice of splittings can be compatible with $f^*$.

blocks.body:
- $H^n(X;G)$ is an extension of $\mathrm{Hom}(H_nX,G)$ by $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}X,G)$, natural in $X$, split but not naturally split.
- Integrally, free parts stay and torsion moves up one degree; $H^1(X;G)=\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1X,G)$.
- Field coefficients: cohomology is the dual of homology with the same coefficients; over $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ torsion disappears.
- Cellular cochains compute $H^*$ of CW complexes; $\mathbb{RP}^n$ has $H^k(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $0\le k\le n$.

blocks.title: The cup product
blocks.body:
After this section you can compute cup products of explicit cocycles on a triangulated space and use them, through naturality, to prove that two spaces with the same cohomology groups are different.

Functions on the vertices of a complex can be multiplied pointwise, and the product of two cocycles in degree $0$ (locally constant functions) is again one. To multiply a $1$-cochain $\varphi$ by a $1$-cochain $\psi$ we need a number for each triangle $[v_0,v_1,v_2]$, built from one edge for each factor. The vertex order offers a canonical choice: give $\varphi$ the front edge $[v_0,v_1]$ and $\psi$ the back edge $[v_1,v_2]$, which share the middle vertex. In general a $(k+l)$-simplex has a front $k$-face on its first $k+1$ vertices and a back $l$-face on its last $l+1$ vertices, overlapping in one vertex.

blocks.title: Cup product of cochains
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. For $\varphi\in C^k(X;R)$ and $\psi\in C^l(X;R)$ the cup product $\varphi\smile\psi\in C^{k+l}(X;R)$ is
$$(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)=\varphi\big(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_k]}\big)\cdot\psi\big(\sigma|_{[v_k,\dots,v_{k+l}]}\big)$$
for every singular simplex $\sigma\colon[v_0,\dots,v_{k+l}]\to X$, where $\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_k]}$ is the restriction to the front face (composed with the linear identification with $\Delta^k$) and $\sigma|_{[v_k,\dots,v_{k+l}]}$ the restriction to the back face. The same formula defines the cup product of simplicial cochains on a simplicial complex with ordered vertices, or on a $\Delta$-complex, where each simplex comes with its own vertex order.

On indicator cochains of a simplicial complex this reads (Contessoto et al.)
$$[a_0,\dots,a_k]^*\smile[b_0,\dots,b_l]^*=\begin{cases}[a_0,\dots,a_k,b_1,\dots,b_l]^*&\text{if }a_k=b_0\text{ and this is a simplex},\\0&\text{otherwise:}\end{cases}$$
the product of two simplices is their concatenation along a shared last/first vertex.

In words: evaluate the first cochain on the front face, the second on the back face, and multiply.

blocks.caption: The cup product of two $1$-cochains on a $2$-simplex $[v_0,v_1,v_2]$: $\varphi$ is evaluated on the front edge $[v_0,v_1]$, $\psi$ on the back edge $[v_1,v_2]$; the edge $[v_0,v_2]$ is not used. The vertex order matters: this is why lattice models need a branching structure.
blocks.alt: A triangle with vertices v0 at bottom left, v1 at top, v2 at bottom right. The edge from v0 to v1 is drawn thick and solid, labelled phi, front face. The edge from v1 to v2 is drawn thick and dashed, labelled psi, back face. The bottom edge from v0 to v2 is thin and grey. Arrows on the edges point from lower to higher index.

blocks.title: Leibniz rule and the cohomology ring
blocks.body:
1. (Hatcher, Lemma 3.6.) For $\varphi\in C^k(X;R)$ and $\psi\in C^l(X;R)$,
$$\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile\psi+(-1)^k\,\varphi\smile\delta\psi.$$
2. Consequently the cup product of cocycles is a cocycle, and the product of a cocycle with a coboundary (in either order) is a coboundary, so there is a well-defined bilinear product
$$\smile\colon H^k(X;R)\times H^l(X;R)\to H^{k+l}(X;R),\qquad[\varphi]\smile[\psi]=[\varphi\smile\psi].$$
3. The product is associative and distributive, and the class $1\in H^0(X;R)$ of the constant $0$-cochain with value $1$ is a two-sided unit. So $H^*(X;R)$ is a graded ring (a graded $R$-algebra).
4. Naturality: for $f\colon X\to Y$, $f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b$; so $f^*\colon H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a homomorphism of graded rings, and homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic cohomology rings.
5. Relative products: the same formula gives
$$H^k(X,A;R)\times H^l(X;R)\to H^{k+l}(X,A;R)$$
and
$$H^k(X;R)\times H^l(X,A;R)\to H^{k+l}(X,A;R),$$
and, for $A$, $B$ open in $X$ (or subcomplexes of a CW complex),
$$\begin{aligned}H^k(X,A;R)&\times H^l(X,B;R)\\&\to H^{k+l}(X,A\cup B;R)\end{aligned}.$$
They are natural for maps of pairs and compatible with the maps forgetting $A$ or $B$.

Idea for 1: expand both terms on a $(k+l+1)$-simplex; one term from each sum cancels and the rest is $(\varphi\smile\psi)(\partial\sigma)$.

1. Let $\sigma\colon[v_0,\dots,v_{k+l+1}]\to X$. Write $\sigma_{\hat\imath}$ for the face omitting $v_i$, and $\sigma|_{[\dots]}$ for restrictions. Then
$$(\delta\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{k+1}(-1)^i\varphi\big(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,\hat v_i,\dots,v_{k+1}]}\big)\,\psi\big(\sigma|_{[v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l+1}]}\big),$$
$$(-1)^k(\varphi\smile\delta\psi)(\sigma)=\sum_{i=k}^{k+l+1}(-1)^i\varphi\big(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_k]}\big)\,\psi\big(\sigma|_{[v_k,\dots,\hat v_i,\dots,v_{k+l+1}]}\big),$$
where in the second line $\delta\psi$ evaluated on the back face $[v_k,\dots,v_{k+l+1}]$ has the sign $(-1)^{i-k}$ for omitting $v_i$, and $(-1)^k(-1)^{i-k}=(-1)^i$. The last term of the first sum ($i=k+1$) is $(-1)^{k+1}\varphi(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_k]})\psi(\sigma|_{[v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l+1}]})$ and the first term of the second ($i=k$) is the same product with sign $(-1)^k$; they cancel. The remaining terms are, for $i\le k$, $(-1)^i(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma_{\hat\imath})$ (the front $k$-face of $\sigma_{\hat\imath}$ is $[v_0,\dots,\hat v_i,\dots,v_{k+1}]$ and its back $l$-face is $[v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l+1}]$), and for $i\ge k+1$, again $(-1)^i(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma_{\hat\imath})$ (front face $[v_0,\dots,v_k]$, back face $[v_k,\dots,\hat v_i,\dots,v_{k+l+1}]$). Their sum is $(\varphi\smile\psi)(\partial\sigma)=\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)$.

2. If $\delta\varphi=\delta\psi=0$ then $\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=0$. If $\delta\varphi=0$ and $\psi=\delta\eta$, then $\delta(\varphi\smile\eta)=(-1)^k\varphi\smile\psi$, a coboundary; similarly $\delta\eta\smile\psi=\delta(\eta\smile\psi)$ when $\delta\psi=0$. So the class of $\varphi\smile\psi$ depends only on the classes; bilinearity holds already for cochains.

3. Associativity holds for cochains: $((\varphi\smile\psi)\smile\chi)(\sigma)$ and $(\varphi\smile(\psi\smile\chi))(\sigma)$ both equal $\varphi(\sigma|_{[v_0..v_k]})\psi(\sigma|_{[v_k..v_{k+l}]})\chi(\sigma|_{[v_{k+l}..v_{k+l+m}]})$. For the unit, the front or back $0$-face of $\sigma$ is a point where $1$ takes the value $1$.

4.
$$\begin{aligned}(f^\sharp\varphi\smile f^\sharp\psi)(\sigma)&=\varphi(f\sigma|_{\text{front}})\,\psi(f\sigma|_{\text{back}})\\&=f^\sharp(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)\end{aligned},$$
since restricting to a face commutes with composing with $f$.

5. If $\varphi$ vanishes on simplices in $A$, so does $\varphi\smile\psi$, because the front face of a simplex in $A$ lies in $A$; similarly for $\psi$ and back faces. This gives the first two products. For the third, the formula gives a product into cochains vanishing on sums of chains in $A$ and chains in $B$, and the inclusion of the cochains vanishing on $A\cup B$ into these induces an isomorphism on cohomology when $A$, $B$ are open; this uses the small-chains theorem, Lemma 1 and the five lemma (Quick, Lecture 21; Hatcher §3.2).

blocks.title: The cup product on the torus, by hand
blocks.body: Use the $\Delta$-complex of the torus from [[homology]]: a square with corners $bl,br,tr,tl$, horizontal sides $a$ (left to right), vertical sides $b$ (upwards), diagonal $c$ from $bl$ to $tr$, and triangles $U=[bl,br,tr]$, $L=[bl,tl,tr]$; all four corners are one vertex $v$. Find cocycles $\alpha,\beta$ representing a basis of $H^1(T^2;\mathbb{Z})$, show that evaluation on the cycle $U-L$ identifies $H^2(T^2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, and compute all products $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$, $\alpha\beta$, $\beta\alpha$.
blocks.solution:
Faces. In $U=[bl,br,tr]$: the front edge is $[bl,br]=a$, the back edge $[br,tr]=b$, and $\partial U=b-c+a$. In $L=[bl,tl,tr]$: the front edge is $[bl,tl]=b$, the back edge $[tl,tr]=a$, and $\partial L=a-c+b$.

$H^1$. There is one vertex, so $\delta f(e)=f(v)-f(v)=0$ for every edge: $B^1=0$. A $1$-cochain $\varphi$ is a cocycle iff $\varphi(b)-\varphi(c)+\varphi(a)=0$ (the condition from $U$; $L$ gives the same), i.e. $\varphi(c)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$. So $H^1=Z^1\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$, with basis
$$\alpha:\ (a,b,c)\mapsto(1,0,1),\qquad\beta:\ (a,b,c)\mapsto(0,1,1).$$
$\alpha$ is dual to $a$ ($\alpha(a)=1$, $\alpha(b)=0$) and $\beta$ dual to $b$.

$H^2$. $C^2=\mathbb{Z}^2$ (values on $U$, $L$), and $\delta\varphi=(\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)-\varphi(c))(U^*+L^*)$, so $B^2=\{tU^*+tL^*\}$. The map $\omega\mapsto\omega(U-L)=\omega(U)-\omega(L)$ is onto $\mathbb{Z}$ with kernel exactly $B^2$, so $H^2\cong\mathbb{Z}$; $U-L$ is the fundamental cycle found on [[homology]].

Products, by front face times back face:
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha\smile\beta)(U)&=\alpha(a)\beta(b)=1,&(\alpha\smile\beta)(L)&=\alpha(b)\beta(a)=0,\\(\beta\smile\alpha)(U)&=\beta(a)\alpha(b)=0,&(\beta\smile\alpha)(L)&=\beta(b)\alpha(a)=1,\\(\alpha\smile\alpha)(U)&=\alpha(a)\alpha(b)=0,&(\alpha\smile\alpha)(L)&=\alpha(b)\alpha(a)=0,\end{aligned}$$
and likewise $\beta\smile\beta$ vanishes on $U$ and $L$. Evaluating on $U-L$: $\alpha\beta\mapsto1$, $\beta\alpha\mapsto-1$, $\alpha^2,\beta^2\mapsto0$. So $\alpha\beta=\gamma$ is a generator of $H^2(T^2;\mathbb{Z})$, $\beta\alpha=-\gamma$, $\alpha^2=\beta^2=0$:
$$H^*(T^2;\mathbb{Z})=\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha,\beta],$$
the exterior algebra on two generators of degree $1$ (Quick, Lecture 21).

Note that the cochains $\alpha\smile\beta=U^*$ and $-\beta\smile\alpha=-L^*$ are different; they differ by $U^*+L^*=\delta(a^*)$, a coboundary. Commutativity up to sign holds only in cohomology.

Geometrically, $\alpha$ takes the value $1$ exactly on the edges crossed by a vertical loop (it crosses $a$ and $c$ but not $b$), and $\beta$ on the edges crossed by a horizontal loop. The two loops cross once, and the product $\alpha\beta$ is a generator: this is Hatcher's picture of cup products of degree-one classes on surfaces as intersections of transverse curves.

blocks.caption: The $\Delta$-complex of the torus with triangles $U$ and $L$. The cocycle $\alpha$ is $1$ on the edges $a$ and $c$, which the vertical loop (red, dashed) crosses; $\beta$ is $1$ on $b$ and $c$, which the horizontal loop (blue, dotted) crosses. The loops meet once, and $\alpha\smile\beta$ generates $H^2$.
blocks.alt: A square with corners labelled bl, br, tr, tl. Bottom and top edges labelled a with arrows to the right; left and right edges labelled b with arrows upwards; a diagonal labelled c from bottom left to top right. Triangle U is below the diagonal, triangle L above it. A red dashed vertical line crosses the bottom edge, the diagonal and the top edge; a blue dotted horizontal line crosses the left edge, the diagonal and the right edge. They cross at one point.

blocks.title: The Klein bottle mod 2: same groups as the torus, different ring
blocks.body: Use the $\Delta$-complex of the Klein bottle $K$ from [[homology]]: the same square with the left side $b$ running upwards and the right side $b$ running downwards, diagonal $c$ from $tl$ to $br$, triangles $U=[tl,tr,br]$ and $L=[bl,tl,br]$, one vertex. Compute the ring $H^*(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and compare it with $H^*(T^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
blocks.solution:
Faces. In $U=[tl,tr,br]$: front edge $[tl,tr]=a$, back edge $[tr,br]=b$, $\partial U=b-c+a$. In $L=[bl,tl,br]$: front edge $[bl,tl]=b$, back edge $[tl,br]=c$, $\partial L=c-a+b$. Mod $2$ both cocycle conditions read $\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)+\varphi(c)=0$, and again $B^1=0$. So $H^1(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ with basis
$$x:\ (a,b,c)\mapsto(1,0,1),\qquad y:\ (a,b,c)\mapsto(0,1,1).$$
$H^2(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $\omega\mapsto\omega(U)+\omega(L)$ ($B^2$ is spanned by $U^*+L^*$; $U+L$ is a cycle mod $2$). Let $w$ be the generator.

Products (front value times back value on $U$, then on $L$):
$$\begin{aligned}x^2&:\ x(a)x(b)+x(b)x(c)=0+0=0,\\y^2&:\ y(a)y(b)+y(b)y(c)=0+1=1,\\xy&:\ x(a)y(b)+x(b)y(c)=1+0=1,\\yx&:\ y(a)x(b)+y(b)x(c)=0+1=1.\end{aligned}$$
So $x^2=0$ and $xy=yx=y^2=w$.

On the torus mod $2$, the computation of the previous example reduced mod $2$ gives $\alpha^2=\beta^2=0$ and $\alpha\beta=\beta\alpha=w$; then every class squares to zero, since $(s\alpha+t\beta)^2=s^2\alpha^2+t^2\beta^2+2st\,\alpha\beta=0$. On the Klein bottle $(sx+ty)^2=t\,w$ (the cross terms cancel in pairs mod 2) is nonzero whenever $t\neq0$. So the two rings are not isomorphic although the groups agree ($\mathbb{Z}/2$, $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, $\mathbb{Z}/2$). Hatcher's geometric reading: on a nonorientable surface a curve whose neighbourhood is a Möbius band cannot be pushed off itself, and this is why some degree-one class has nonzero square mod $2$. Contessoto et al. use this mod $2$ ring of the Klein bottle in their persistent cup-length examples.

blocks.title: Hatcher's example: a product that only Z/m sees
blocks.body: Let $X_m=S^1\cup_me^2$ ($m\ge2$) as in the section on coefficients. Build it as a $\Delta$-complex (Hatcher, Example 3.9): a regular $m$-gon cut into $m$ triangles $T_i=[v,w_i,w_{i+1}]$ ($i=0,\dots,m-1$, indices mod $m$) around a centre $v$; all outer vertices $w_i$ are identified to one vertex $w$, all outer edges $[w_i,w_{i+1}]$ to one edge $e$ (a loop at $w$), and the spokes $e_i=[v,w_i]$ remain distinct. Show that $H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)\cong\mathbb{Z}/m$ with generator $\alpha$ given by $\varphi(e)=1$, $\varphi(e_i)=i$, that $H^2(X_m;\mathbb{Z}/m)\cong\mathbb{Z}/m$ by evaluation on $\sum_iT_i$, and that $\alpha^2=0$ for $m$ odd while $\alpha^2=k\beta$ for $m=2k$, where $\beta$ is the generator with value $1$ on $\sum_iT_i$.
blocks.solution:
The complex has $2$ vertices, $m+1$ edges and $m$ triangles ($\chi=1$), and $\partial T_i=e-e_{i+1}+e_i$.

$H^1$. A $1$-cochain $\varphi$ is a cocycle iff $\varphi(e)-\varphi(e_{i+1})+\varphi(e_i)=0$ for all $i$, i.e. $\varphi(e_{i+1})=\varphi(e_i)+\varphi(e)$. This determines $\varphi$ from $\varphi(e_0)$ and $\varphi(e)$, and going once round gives $\varphi(e_0)=\varphi(e_0)+m\varphi(e)$, which holds in $\mathbb{Z}/m$. So $Z^1\cong(\mathbb{Z}/m)^2$. Coboundaries: $(\delta f)(e_i)=f(w)-f(v)$ and $(\delta f)(e)=0$, so $B^1$ is the line $\varphi(e)=0$, $\varphi(e_i)=t$ constant. Hence $H^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/m$ via $[\varphi]\mapsto\varphi(e)$, generated by $\alpha=[\varphi]$ with $\varphi(e)=1$, $\varphi(e_i)=i$.

$H^2$. $\partial\sum_iT_i=me-\sum_ie_{i+1}+\sum_ie_i=me=0$ mod $m$, so evaluation on $c=\sum_iT_i$ kills coboundaries. It is onto. The map $\delta\colon C^1=(\mathbb{Z}/m)^{m+1}\to C^2=(\mathbb{Z}/m)^m$ has kernel $Z^1$ of order $m^2$, so its image has order $m^{m-1}$, which is the order of the kernel of evaluation; hence $B^2=\ker(\mathrm{ev}_c)$ and $H^2\cong\mathbb{Z}/m$.

The square. The front edge of $T_i$ is $[v,w_i]=e_i$ and the back edge is $[w_i,w_{i+1}]=e$, so $(\varphi\smile\varphi)(T_i)=\varphi(e_i)\varphi(e)=i$ and
$$(\varphi\smile\varphi)(c)=0+1+\cdots+(m-1)=\frac{m(m-1)}2\pmod m.$$
If $m$ is odd, $(m-1)/2$ is an integer and this is $0$ mod $m$. If $m=2k$, it is $k(2k-1)=2k^2-k\equiv-k\equiv k\pmod{2k}$. So $\alpha^2=0$ for $m$ odd and $\alpha^2=k\beta$ for $m=2k$. For $m=2$, $X_2=\mathbb{RP}^2$ and $\alpha^2=\beta\neq0$ in $H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.

With integer coefficients nothing of this is visible: $H^1(X_m;\mathbb{Z})=0$, so all products of degree-one integral classes vanish. The ring structure with $\mathbb{Z}/m$ coefficients carries information that the integral ring does not.
