The generator of $H^1(X_4;\mathbb{Z}/4)$ takes the value $1$ on $e$ and $i$ on the spoke $e_i$; its square takes the value $i$ on $T_i$.
blocks.alt: A square with a centre point v joined by four spokes to the corners w0, w1, w2, w3. Each outer side is labelled e with an arrow pointing counterclockwise. Spokes are labelled e0 = 0, e1 = 1, e2 = 2, e3 = 3, the values of the cocycle. The four triangles are labelled T0 to T3.

blocks.title: The cup product, four ways
blocks.body: All four descriptions produce the same ring $H^*(X;R)$ (up to the sign conventions tabulated below); papers use whichever matches their tools.

items.label: Front face, back face
items.body: Evaluate $\varphi$ on the front $k$-face and $\psi$ on the back $l$-face of each simplex and multiply. On a simplicial complex this is concatenation of simplices sharing a last and first vertex, which Contessoto et al. implement directly in their cup-length algorithm.

items.label: Cross product and diagonal
items.body: Miller first builds the cross product $H^p(X)\otimes H^q(Y)\to H^{p+q}(X\times Y)$ from the Alexander–Whitney map $C_\bullet(X\times Y)\to C_\bullet(X)\otimes C_\bullet(Y)$ (front face to the first factor, back face to the second), and defines $a\smile b=\Delta^*(a\times b)$ for the diagonal $\Delta\colon X\to X\times X$. Wikipedia notes that this is why products exist in cohomology but not in homology: the diagonal pulls back, it does not push forward a product.

items.label: Intersecting dual curves
items.body: On a surface a degree-one class can be represented by a cocycle counting crossings with a transverse curve, and the product of two classes evaluates on the fundamental class to the signed number of intersection points. Chen and Tata picture a $p$-cochain on a lattice as a $(d-p)$-dimensional surface on the dual cellulation, with cup product becoming intersection after a small shift; making this precise is Poincaré duality, a separate topic.

items.label: Wedge of forms
items.body: On a smooth manifold with real coefficients, de Rham's theorem ([[de-rham-cohomology]]) identifies $H^*(M;\mathbb{R})$ with closed forms modulo exact forms, and the cup product with the wedge product: $[\omega]\smile[\eta]=[\omega\wedge\eta]$.

items.q: On the filled triangle, compute $[0,1]^*\smile[1,2]^*$ and $[1,2]^*\smile[0,1]^*$.
items.a: $[0,1]^*\smile[1,2]^*=[0,1,2]^*$ (concatenation along the vertex $1$); $[1,2]^*\smile[0,1]^*=0$, since $2\ne0$ and no simplex has front edge $[1,2]$.

items.q: Why must the cup product of any two classes of positive degree vanish on $S^n$, $n\ge1$?
items.a: The product lands in degree at least $2n$ or in a degree between $n+1$ and $2n-1$; all these groups are zero.

items.q: Why does a nonzero product $a\smile b\in H^2$ of two degree-one classes show that a space is not homotopy equivalent to a wedge of circles and $2$-spheres?
items.a: In such a wedge all products of degree-one classes vanish (each degree-one class lives on one circle, whose $H^2$ is $0$), and a homotopy equivalence induces a ring isomorphism.

items.q: On $\Delta^3=[0,1,2,3]$ with integer coefficients let $\varphi=[0,1]^*$ and $\psi=[1,2]^*$. Compute $\varphi\smile\psi$, $\delta\varphi$, $\delta\psi$, and check the Leibniz rule $\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile\psi-\varphi\smile\delta\psi$ on $[0,1,2,3]$.
items.hint: Use the formula for $\delta$ of an indicator cochain (sign $(-1)^i$ for the position $i$ of the added vertex) and concatenation for products.
items.solution: $\varphi\smile\psi=[0,1,2]^*$. Its only coface is $[0,1,2,3]$, with the added vertex $3$ in position $3$, so $\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=-[0,1,2,3]^*$. Next $\delta\varphi=[0,1,2]^*+[0,1,3]^*$ (added vertex in position $2$ both times) and $\delta\psi=[0,1,2]^*+[1,2,3]^*$ (positions $0$ and $2$). On $[0,1,2,3]$: $(\delta\varphi\smile\psi)=\delta\varphi[0,1,2]\,\psi[2,3]=1\cdot0=0$ and $(\varphi\smile\delta\psi)=\varphi[0,1]\,\delta\psi[1,2,3]=1\cdot1=1$. So the right side is $0-1=-1$, equal to the left side.

items.q: On $\Delta^2$ let $f$ be the $0$-cochain with $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=2$ and $\psi=[1,2]^*$. Verify $\delta(f\smile\psi)=\delta f\smile\psi+f\smile\delta\psi$ on $[0,1,2]$.
items.hint: $(f\smile\psi)[i,j]=f(i)\psi[i,j]$ and $(\delta f\smile\psi)[0,1,2]=\delta f[0,1]\,\psi[1,2]$.
items.solution: $f\smile\psi$ is the $1$-cochain $[i,j]\mapsto f(i)\psi[i,j]$, which is $1\cdot1=1$ on $[1,2]$ and $0$ elsewhere, i.e. $[1,2]^*$. So $\delta(f\smile\psi)[0,1,2]=\delta[1,2]^*[0,1,2]=1$. On the right, $(\delta f\smile\psi)[0,1,2]=(f(1)-f(0))\psi[1,2]=1$ and $(f\smile\delta\psi)[0,1,2]=f(0)\,\delta\psi[0,1,2]=0$. Both sides equal $1$.

items.q: Show that in $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$ all products of classes of positive degree vanish, and conclude (with the torus example) that $T^2\not\simeq S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$ although their cohomology groups agree.
items.hint: Restrict to the wedge summands; for CW complexes, $\tilde H^*$ of a wedge is the product of the $\tilde H^*$ of the summands, and the restriction maps are ring homomorphisms.
items.solution: Let $X=S^1_1\vee S^1_2\vee S^2$ and $i_j$ the inclusions of the summands. The map $\tilde H^n(X)\to\prod_j\tilde H^n(\text{summand}_j)$, $a\mapsto(i_j^*a)_j$, is an isomorphism (Mayer–Vietoris, or Hatcher Example 3.14). For $a,b\in H^1(X)$, $i_j^*(ab)=i_j^*a\,i_j^*b$ lies in $H^2$ of a circle (zero) or is a product of classes in $H^1(S^2)=0$. So all components of $ab$ vanish and $ab=0$. Products involving $H^2$ land in degree $\ge3$, which is zero. On $T^2$, $\alpha\beta$ generates $H^2$. A homotopy equivalence would induce a ring isomorphism, impossible.

items.q: Using Hatcher's $\Delta$-complex, compute $\alpha^2$ in $H^2(X_3;\mathbb{Z}/3)$ and in $H^2(X_4;\mathbb{Z}/4)$ directly, listing the value of $\varphi\smile\varphi$ on each triangle.
items.hint: $(\varphi\smile\varphi)(T_i)=\varphi(e_i)\varphi(e)=i$.
items.solution: $m=3$: values $0,1,2$ on $T_0,T_1,T_2$, total $3\equiv0$ mod $3$, so $\alpha^2=0$. $m=4$: values $0,1,2,3$, total $6\equiv2$ mod $4$, so $\alpha^2=2\beta$, nonzero, in agreement with $k=2$.

items.q: Let $M_2$ be the closed orientable surface of genus $2$ and $q\colon M_2\to T^2\vee T^2$ the map collapsing a separating circle. Granting (Hatcher §3.2) that $q^*$ is an isomorphism on $H^1(-;\mathbb{Z})$, that $H^2(M_2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ with generator $\gamma$, and that $q^*$ sends the generator $\gamma_j$ of $H^2$ of each torus summand to $\gamma$, compute the ring $H^*(M_2;\mathbb{Z})$ in the basis $\alpha_j=q^*a_j$, $\beta_j=q^*b_j$ ($j=1,2$), where $a_j,b_j$ are the classes $\alpha,\beta$ of the $j$-th torus.
items.hint: Compute the ring of $T^2\vee T^2$ from the two summands (products of classes from different summands vanish) and pull back with the ring homomorphism $q^*$.
items.solution: $\tilde H^*(T^2\vee T^2)\cong\tilde H^*(T^2)\times\tilde H^*(T^2)$ as rings, so $a_jb_j=\gamma_j=-b_ja_j$, $a_j^2=b_j^2=0$, and any product of a class from the first summand with one from the second is $0$. Applying the ring homomorphism $q^*$: $\alpha_j\beta_j=q^*\gamma_j=\gamma$ and $\beta_j\alpha_j=-\gamma$ for $j=1,2$; $\alpha_j^2=\beta_j^2=0$; and $\alpha_1\alpha_2=\alpha_1\beta_2=\beta_1\alpha_2=\beta_1\beta_2=0$. So the cup pairing $H^1\times H^1\to H^2\cong\mathbb{Z}$ has, in the basis $\alpha_1,\beta_1,\alpha_2,\beta_2$, the block matrix with two blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$: a symplectic form, as in Hatcher's Example 3.7 for general genus.

blocks.body:
- $(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\sigma_{\mathrm{fr}})\,\psi(\sigma_{\mathrm{bk}})$ (front $k$-face, back $l$-face); on simplicial complexes, concatenation of simplices.
- $\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile\psi+(-1)^k\varphi\smile\delta\psi$, so $\smile$ descends: $H^*(X;R)$ is an associative unital graded ring and $f^*$ is a ring map.
- Torus: $\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha,\beta]$; Klein bottle mod 2: $x^2=0$, $y^2=xy=yx\neq0$; $X_m$ mod $m$: $\alpha^2=k\beta$ for $m=2k$.
- Rings distinguish spaces with equal groups: $T^2$ versus $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$.

blocks.title: Graded commutativity
blocks.body:
After this section you can reorder products in a cohomology ring with the correct signs, predict which squares must vanish, and explain why the cochain-level product is not commutative.

On the torus we found $\beta\alpha=-\alpha\beta$ in cohomology, although the cochains $\alpha\smile\beta$ and $-\beta\smile\alpha$ were different. In degree $0$ the product is the pointwise product of functions and is commutative. The general rule interpolates: classes commute up to the sign $(-1)^{kl}$, the sign one gets by moving a $k$-dimensional object past an $l$-dimensional one.

blocks.title: Graded commutativity
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be commutative. For $a\in H^k(X;R)$ and $b\in H^l(X;R)$,
$$a\smile b=(-1)^{kl}\,b\smile a.$$
The same holds for the relative products. Consequently, if $k$ is odd then $2a^2=0$. Hence $a^2=0$ whenever $2$ is invertible in $R$ (for instance $R=\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R}$ or a field of characteristic $\neq2$), and for $R=\mathbb{Z}$ whenever $H^{2k}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ has no elements of order $2$.

Idea (Hatcher, Theorem 3.11; Quick, Lecture 20): reversing the order of the vertices of every simplex swaps front and back faces. With a suitable sign this reversal is a chain map homotopic to the identity, so it acts trivially on cohomology, while on cochains it turns $\varphi\smile\psi$ into $\pm\psi\smile\varphi$.

Step 1 (the reversal). For a singular $n$-simplex $\sigma$ let $\bar\sigma$ be $\sigma$ precomposed with the linear map $\Delta^n\to\Delta^n$ reversing the vertex order $v_0,\dots,v_n\mapsto v_n,\dots,v_0$. Put
$$\rho(\sigma)=\varepsilon_n\bar\sigma,\qquad\varepsilon_n=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}.$$

Step 2 ($\rho$ is a chain map). The $i$-th vertex of $\bar\sigma$ is $v_{n-i}$, so deleting it is deleting $v_{n-i}$ from $\sigma$: $\partial\bar\sigma=\sum_i(-1)^i\overline{\sigma_{\widehat{n-i}}}=(-1)^n\sum_j(-1)^j\overline{\sigma_{\hat\jmath}}$. Hence $\partial\rho(\sigma)=\varepsilon_n(-1)^n\sum_j(-1)^j\overline{\sigma_{\hat\jmath}}$, while $\rho(\partial\sigma)=\varepsilon_{n-1}\sum_j(-1)^j\overline{\sigma_{\hat\jmath}}$. These agree because $\varepsilon_n=(-1)^n\varepsilon_{n-1}$, as $\tfrac{n(n+1)}2-\tfrac{(n-1)n}2=n$.

Step 3 ($\rho$ is chain homotopic to the identity). Hatcher and Quick write down an explicit chain homotopy $P$ with $\partial P+P\partial=\rho-\mathrm{id}$, a prism operator on $\Delta^n\times I$ whose top vertices are listed in reverse order, with signs $\varepsilon$; the verification is a sign computation of the same kind as for the prism operator of homotopy invariance (Hatcher §3.2, proof of Theorem 3.11). Alternatively, Miller (Lecture 29) indicates the method of acyclic models: $\rho$ and $\mathrm{id}$ are natural chain maps on singular chains that agree in degree $0$ (where $\varepsilon_0=1$ and $\bar\sigma=\sigma$), and the models $\Delta^n$ are contractible, which forces any two such maps to be naturally chain homotopic. Either way, dualising as in homotopy invariance, $\rho^*$ is the identity on $H^*(X;R)$.

Step 4 (the cochain identity). For $\varphi\in C^k$, $\psi\in C^l$ and $\sigma$ a $(k+l)$-simplex,
$$(\rho^*\varphi\smile\rho^*\psi)(\sigma)=\varepsilon_k\varepsilon_l\,\varphi\big(\sigma|_{[v_k,\dots,v_0]}\big)\,\psi\big(\sigma|_{[v_{k+l},\dots,v_k]}\big),$$
because the front face of $\sigma$ is $[v_0,\dots,v_k]$ and $\rho$ reverses it. On the other hand the front $l$-face of $\bar\sigma=[v_{k+l},\dots,v_0]$ is $[v_{k+l},\dots,v_k]$ and its back $k$-face is $[v_k,\dots,v_0]$, so
$$\rho^*(\psi\smile\varphi)(\sigma)=\varepsilon_{k+l}\,\psi\big(\sigma|_{[v_{k+l},\dots,v_k]}\big)\,\varphi\big(\sigma|_{[v_k,\dots,v_0]}\big).$$
Since $R$ is commutative and $\varepsilon_{k+l}=(-1)^{kl}\varepsilon_k\varepsilon_l$ (because $\tfrac{(k+l)(k+l+1)}2=\tfrac{k(k+1)}2+\tfrac{l(l+1)}2+kl$), we get $\rho^*\varphi\smile\rho^*\psi=(-1)^{kl}\rho^*(\psi\smile\varphi)$.

Step 5. For cocycles, pass to cohomology, where $\rho^*=\mathrm{id}$: $a\smile b=(-1)^{kl}b\smile a$. For $a=b$ of odd degree $k$, $a^2=(-1)^{k^2}a^2=-a^2$, so $2a^2=0$. If $2$ is invertible in $R$, multiply by $\tfrac12$ to get $a^2=0$. For $R=\mathbb{Z}$ the conclusion is only $2a^2=0$: $a^2$ is an element of order at most $2$ in $H^{2k}(X;\mathbb{Z})$, which forces $a^2=0$ when that group has no $2$-torsion. (Quick's Lecture 20 phrases the last step for torsion-free $R$; what is needed is the absence of $2$-torsion in the group $H^{2k}$.)

- Graded commutativity is a statement about cohomology classes. On cochains the cup product is not commutative even up to sign: on the torus $\alpha\smile\beta=U^*$ and $-\beta\smile\alpha=-L^*$ differ by the coboundary $U^*+L^*$. Miller stresses that the cochain product is 'clearly not' graded commutative; over $\mathbb{Q}$ there are commutative cochain models (Sullivan), but in positive characteristic Steenrod operations obstruct them.
- Odd-degree classes need not square to zero mod $2$: $x^2\neq0$ for the generator of $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$, and $y^2\ne0$ on the Klein bottle. Over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ the sign is invisible and the ring is simply commutative.
- With integer coefficients, $2a^2=0$ for odd $a$ does not give $a^2=0$ if $H^{2k}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ has $2$-torsion. The step from $2a^2=0$ to $a^2=0$ needs the group $H^{2k}$, not only the ring $R$, to have no $2$-torsion; with $R=\mathbb{Q}$ or a field of characteristic $\ne2$ that is automatic.
- On a simplicial complex the cup product depends on the vertex order (the branching structure of Chen and Tata); different orders give cohomologous cochains, but explicit cocycle formulas in papers are tied to the chosen order.

blocks.title: The cup-1 product measures non-commutativity
blocks.body:
With $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients on an ordered simplicial complex, define for a $p$-cochain $\alpha$ and a $q$-cochain $\beta$ the $(p+q-1)$-cochain
$$(\alpha\smile_1\beta)(0,\dots,p+q-1)=\sum_{0\le i<j\le p+q-1}\alpha(0\to i,\ j\to p+q-1)\,\beta(i\to j),$$
where $\alpha(0\to i,\ j\to p+q-1)$ means $\alpha$ evaluated on the face with vertices $0,\dots,i,j,\dots,p+q-1$ (which must have $p+1$ vertices) and $\beta(i\to j)$ on the face with vertices $i,\dots,j$ (which must have $q+1$ vertices); terms with the wrong number of vertices are omitted (Chen–Tata, Eq. (7)). Then for cocycles $\alpha,\beta$,
$$\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)=\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha.$$
So $\alpha\smile\beta$ and $\beta\smile\alpha$ are cohomologous mod $2$, with an explicit cochain between them.

The general statement is Steenrod's coboundary formula
$$\begin{aligned}\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)={}&\delta\alpha\smile_1\beta+\alpha\smile_1\delta\beta\\&+\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha\end{aligned}$$
mod $2$, which Chen and Tata state as their Eq. (9) (in their Proposition 2 the second term is printed slightly differently; for cocycles both versions give the same conclusion). The page's checks verify the formula on random cochains of a $6$-simplex. Here is the case $p=q=1$ by hand. The only pair is $i=0$, $j=1$, so $(\alpha\smile_1\beta)(01)=\alpha(01)\beta(01)$: the cup-1 product of two $1$-cochains is their edgewise product. On a triangle,
$$\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)(012)=\alpha(12)\beta(12)+\alpha(02)\beta(02)+\alpha(01)\beta(01).$$
If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are cocycles, $\alpha(02)=\alpha(01)+\alpha(12)$ and $\beta(02)=\beta(01)+\beta(12)$, so the middle term expands to
$$\begin{aligned}&\alpha(01)\beta(01)+\alpha(01)\beta(12)\\&+\alpha(12)\beta(01)+\alpha(12)\beta(12)\end{aligned},$$
and mod $2$ the sum becomes
$$\begin{aligned}&\alpha(01)\beta(12)+\alpha(12)\beta(01)\\&=(\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha)(012)\end{aligned}.$$

items.q: Is $H^*(T^2;\mathbb{Z})$ a commutative ring?
items.a: No: $\beta\alpha=-\alpha\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ generates $H^2\cong\mathbb{Z}$, so $\alpha\beta\neq\beta\alpha$. It is graded commutative.

items.q: In which degrees must every class square to zero in $H^*(X;\mathbb{Q})$?
items.a: In odd degrees: $a^2=-a^2$ gives $2a^2=0$, and $H^*(X;\mathbb{Q})$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space.

items.q: Why is $\rho$ the identity in degree $0$, and why does that matter?
items.a: $\varepsilon_0=1$ and reversing a single vertex does nothing; agreement in degree $0$ is what the acyclic models argument needs to produce a natural chain homotopy $\rho\simeq\mathrm{id}$.

items.q: Verify $\varepsilon_{k+l}=(-1)^{kl}\varepsilon_k\varepsilon_l$ for $\varepsilon_n=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}$, and tabulate $\varepsilon_n$ for $n=0,\dots,7$.
items.hint: Expand $(k+l)(k+l+1)$.
items.solution: $(k+l)(k+l+1)=k(k+1)+l(l+1)+2kl$, so halving gives the exponent identity. The values are $\varepsilon_0,\dots,\varepsilon_7=1,-1,-1,1,1,-1,-1,1$ (period $4$).

items.q: Let $a\in H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$ and $b\in H^3(X;\mathbb{Z})$. Simplify $b\,a\,b$ and $a\,b\,a\,b$.
items.hint: Move factors past each other, collecting $(-1)^{kl}$.
items.solution: $ba=(-1)^6ab=ab$, so $bab=ab^2$; and $b^2$ has odd degree factors: $b^2=(-1)^9b^2=-b^2$, so $2b^2=0$. Then $abab=a(ba)b=a(ab)b=a^2b^2$, with $2a^2b^2=0$.

items.q: On the torus with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients, compute the cochain $\alpha\smile_1\beta$ for the cocycles $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus example, and verify $\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)=\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha$ on $U$ and $L$.
items.hint: For $1$-cochains $\alpha\smile_1\beta$ is the edgewise product. Use the face lists of $U=[bl,br,tr]$ and $L=[bl,tl,tr]$.
items.solution: Edgewise: $\alpha=(1,0,1)$, $\beta=(0,1,1)$ on $(a,b,c)$, so $\alpha\smile_1\beta=(0,0,1)=c^*$. Then $\delta c^*$ on $U$ is $c^*(\partial U)=c^*(b-c+a)=1$ mod $2$, and on $L$ also $1$. On the other side, $(\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha)(U)=1+0=1$ and $(\ldots)(L)=0+1=1$. They agree. (The $\Delta$-complex identifications do not matter here: the formula is applied simplex by simplex with each simplex's own vertex order.)

items.q: Show that if $H^*(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is torsion-free, the subring generated by $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is a quotient of the exterior algebra $\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[H^1]$, i.e. degree-one classes anticommute and square to zero.
items.hint: Graded commutativity with $k=l=1$.
items.solution: For $a,b\in H^1$: $ab=-ba$, and $2a^2=0$ gives $a^2=0$ because $H^2$ is torsion-free. The exterior algebra on the free abelian group $H^1$ (or on generators of it) is the free graded-commutative ring with these relations, so the map $\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[H^1]\to H^*(X;\mathbb{Z})$ extending the inclusion in degree $1$ exists and is a ring homomorphism; its image is the subring generated by $H^1$.

items.q:
Using the formula for $\smile_1$, check by hand on the $3$-simplex $[0,1,2,3]$ that for a $2$-cochain $\alpha$ and a $2$-cochain $\beta$ one gets
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha\smile_1\beta)(0123)={}&\alpha(013)\beta(123)\\&+\alpha(023)\beta(012)\end{aligned}$$
(Chen–Tata, Eq. (8)).
items.hint: Here $p=q=2$, $p+q-1=3$; $\alpha$ needs $3$ vertices from $\{0,\dots,i\}\cup\{j,\dots,3\}$ and $\beta$ needs $3$ vertices from $\{i,\dots,j\}$.
items.solution: $\beta(i\to j)$ has $j-i+1=3$ vertices, so $j=i+2$: the pairs are $(0,2)$ and $(1,3)$. For $(0,2)$: $\alpha$ gets $\{0\}\cup\{2,3\}=023$ and $\beta$ gets $012$. For $(1,3)$: $\alpha$ gets $\{0,1\}\cup\{3\}=013$ and $\beta$ gets $123$. In both cases $\alpha$ indeed has $3$ vertices. Summing gives the stated formula.

blocks.body:
- $a\smile b=(-1)^{kl}b\smile a$ in cohomology; proof: vertex reversal $\rho$ with sign $\varepsilon_n=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}$ is a chain map homotopic to the identity.
- Odd-degree classes satisfy $2a^2=0$; $a^2=0$ needs no $2$-torsion in $H^{2k}$. Mod $2$, squares of degree-one classes can be nonzero.
- Cochain-level cup products are not commutative; mod $2$, $\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)=\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha$ for cocycles.

blocks.title: Products of spaces: the cross product and the Künneth theorem
blocks.body:
After this section you can write down the cohomology ring of a product from the rings of the factors, know when this is allowed, and compute rings of tori, products of spheres, wedges and disjoint unions, and their cup-lengths.

The torus is $S^1\times S^1$, and its ring $\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha,\beta]$ is built from one degree-one class on each factor. In general a class on $X$ and a class on $Y$ can be pulled back to $X\times Y$ along the projections and multiplied there.

blocks.title: Cross product
blocks.body:
Let $p_1\colon X\times Y\to X$ and $p_2\colon X\times Y\to Y$ be the projections. The cross product of $a\in H^k(X;R)$ and $b\in H^l(Y;R)$ is
$$a\times b=p_1^*(a)\smile p_2^*(b)\in H^{k+l}(X\times Y;R).$$
It is bilinear and induces an $R$-linear map
$$\begin{gathered}\mu\colon H^*(X;R)\otimes_RH^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X\times Y;R),\\ a\otimes b\mapsto a\times b.\end{gathered}$$
Make $H^*(X;R)\otimes_RH^*(Y;R)$ a graded ring by
$$(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=(-1)^{|b||c|}\,ac\otimes bd.$$
Then $\mu$ is a ring homomorphism: $(a\times b)(c\times d)=(-1)^{|b||c|}(ac)\times(bd)$. Conversely the cup product is recovered from the cross product as $a\smile b=\Delta^*(a\times b)$ for the diagonal $\Delta\colon X\to X\times X$, which is Miller's definition.

Ring homomorphism: $(a\times b)(c\times d)=p_1^*a\,p_2^*b\,p_1^*c\,p_2^*d$. Moving $p_2^*b$ past $p_1^*c$ costs $(-1)^{|b||c|}$ by graded commutativity, giving $(-1)^{|b||c|}p_1^*(ac)\,p_2^*(bd)=(-1)^{|b||c|}(ac)\times(bd)$, using that $p_i^*$ are ring maps; this is the sign in the tensor product, so $\mu$ is multiplicative. Diagonal: $p_1\Delta=p_2\Delta=\mathrm{id}_X$, so $\Delta^*(a\times b)=\Delta^*p_1^*a\smile\Delta^*p_2^*b=a\smile b$.

blocks.title: Künneth theorem for cohomology rings
blocks.body:
(Hatcher, Theorem 3.15.) Let $X$ and $Y$ be CW complexes and suppose that $H^k(Y;R)$ is a finitely generated free $R$-module for every $k$. Then the cross product
$$\mu\colon H^*(X;R)\otimes_RH^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X\times Y;R)$$
is an isomorphism of graded rings. In particular this holds when $R$ is a field and $H^k(Y;R)$ is finite dimensional for each $k$ (for example $Y$ a finite CW complex).

Relative and reduced forms (Hatcher, Theorem 3.18): for CW pairs $(X,A)$, $(Y,B)$ with $H^k(Y,B;R)$ finitely generated free for all $k$, the relative cross product
$$H^*(X,A;R)\otimes_RH^*(Y,B;R)\to H^*\big(X\times Y,\ A\times Y\cup X\times B;R\big)$$
is an isomorphism; in particular the cross product of generators of $H^i(D^i,\partial D^i;R)$ and $H^j(D^j,\partial D^j;R)$ generates $H^{i+j}(D^{i+j},\partial D^{i+j};R)$, and cross product with a generator of $\tilde H^k(S^k;R)$ gives the suspension isomorphism $\tilde H^n(X;R)\cong\tilde H^{n+k}(\Sigma^kX;R)$ through $X\wedge S^k=\Sigma^kX$.

We give the structure of Hatcher's proof; the details of each step are in Hatcher §3.2 ('A Künneth formula', Theorem 3.15 and Proposition 3.17).

Step 1 (two cohomology theories). Fix $Y$ and define, for CW pairs $(X,A)$,
$$h^n(X,A)=\bigoplus_iH^i(X,A;R)\otimes_RH^{n-i}(Y;R),\qquad k^n(X,A)=H^n(X\times Y,A\times Y;R).$$
The relative cross product $a\otimes b\mapsto p_1^*a\smile p_2^*b$ defines natural maps $\mu\colon h^n(X,A)\to k^n(X,A)$, and one checks that $\mu$ commutes with the connecting maps of the long exact sequences of pairs (extend a cocycle on $A$ to $X$ and use $\delta\psi=0$ for the cocycle on $Y$).

Step 2 (the axioms). Both $h^*$ and $k^*$ are homotopy invariant, satisfy excision and have long exact sequences of pairs. For $k^*$ this is inherited from $X\times Y$. For $h^*$ the long exact sequence is the sequence of $(X,A)$ tensored with $H^{n-i}(Y;R)$, which stays exact because a free module is a direct sum of copies of $R$. Both convert disjoint unions into products; for $h^*$ this needs $(\prod_\alpha M_\alpha)\otimes N\cong\prod_\alpha(M_\alpha\otimes N)$, true because $N=H^{n-i}(Y;R)$ is finitely generated free. This is where the hypothesis on $Y$ enters.

Step 3 (comparison). For $X$ a point, $h^n=H^n(Y)=k^n$ and $\mu$ is the identity. A natural transformation of cohomology theories on CW pairs that is an isomorphism on a point is an isomorphism on all CW pairs (Hatcher, Proposition 3.17): by the five lemma it suffices to treat $A=\varnothing$; for finite-dimensional $X$ one inducts on dimension, using the long exact sequences of $(X^n,X^{n-1})$, excision to reduce to a disjoint union of pairs $(D^n,\partial D^n)$, and the five lemma again for $(D^n,\partial D^n)$, where $D^n$ is contractible and $\partial D^n$ has smaller dimension; the infinite-dimensional case follows because $H^i(X)\to H^i(X^n)$ is an isomorphism for $n$ large compared with $i$.

Step 4 (rings). $\mu$ is multiplicative by the previous proof, so it is a ring isomorphism. The relative version is reduced to the absolute one by collapsing $B$ to a point and using the split long exact sequences of the retraction onto a base point.

blocks.title: Tori and products of spheres
blocks.body:
(a) Show that $H^*(T^n;\mathbb{Z})=\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$ with $|\alpha_i|=1$, and compute the ranks of $H^k(T^n)$.

(b) For $p,q\ge1$ compute the ring $H^*(S^p\times S^q;\mathbb{Z})$, and show that every map $S^{p+q}\to S^p\times S^q$ induces zero on $H^{p+q}$. Conclude that $S^p\times S^q\not\simeq S^p\vee S^q\vee S^{p+q}$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $H^*(S^1;\mathbb{Z})=\Lambda_{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha]=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\alpha$ is finitely generated free in each degree, so Künneth applies with $Y=S^1$. Inductively,
$$H^*(T^n)\cong H^*(T^{n-1})\otimes H^*(S^1)\cong\Lambda[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{n-1}]\otimes\Lambda[\alpha_n]\cong\Lambda[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n],$$
where $\alpha_i=p_i^*(\alpha)$ for the $i$-th projection $p_i\colon T^n\to S^1$; the last isomorphism holds because the tensor product sign rule makes $\alpha_n$ anticommute with the odd generators. A basis of $H^k$ is $\{\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_k}:i_1<\dots<i_k\}$, so $\operatorname{rank}H^k(T^n)=\binom nk$; for $T^3$: $1,3,3,1$. The top class $\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_n$ generates $H^n(T^n)\cong\mathbb{Z}$.

(b) $H^*(S^p)=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}x$ with $|x|=p$ and $x^2=0$ (degree reasons) is free, so $H^*(S^p\times S^q)$ has basis $1,\ a=x\times1,\ b=1\times y,\ ab=x\times y$ in degrees $0,p,q,p+q$, with $a^2=b^2=0$ and $ab=(-1)^{pq}ba$ (Miller, Example 29.3). Let $f\colon S^{p+q}\to S^p\times S^q$. Then $f^*a\in H^p(S^{p+q})=0$ and $f^*b\in H^q(S^{p+q})=0$ (as $p,q<p+q$), so $f^*(ab)=f^*a\,f^*b=0$; since $ab$ generates $H^{p+q}$, $f^*=0$ in degree $p+q$ (Miller, Corollary 29.4). In the wedge $W=S^p\vee S^q\vee S^{p+q}$ the groups are the same. But $W$ contains $S^{p+q}$ as a summand, and the inclusion $i\colon S^{p+q}\to W$ induces an isomorphism on $H^{p+q}$. If $h\colon W\to S^p\times S^q$ were a homotopy equivalence, $h\circ i$ would be a map $S^{p+q}\to S^p\times S^q$ inducing an isomorphism on $H^{p+q}$, contradicting what we just proved. (In ring terms: in $W$ the product of the degree-$p$ and degree-$q$ classes is zero.)

blocks.title: Disjoint unions and wedges
blocks.body:
(Hatcher, Example 3.14.) For a disjoint union, $H^*(\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha;R)\cong\prod_\alpha H^*(X_\alpha;R)$ as rings, with componentwise multiplication. For a wedge of spaces whose base points are deformation retracts of neighbourhoods (for example CW complexes with base points at vertices), restriction to the summands gives a ring isomorphism
$$\tilde H^*\Big(\bigvee_\alpha X_\alpha;R\Big)\cong\prod_\alpha\tilde H^*(X_\alpha;R);$$
products of classes coming from different summands vanish. Contessoto et al. record the consequence for cup-lengths: they take the maximum over the pieces, while for products they add.

Disjoint unions: the isomorphism of property 6 is restriction to each $X_\alpha$, and restrictions are ring homomorphisms. Wedges: the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence for neighbourhoods $U_\alpha$ deformation retracting to the summands, overlapping in a contractible neighbourhood of the base point, shows that $(i_\alpha^*)\colon\tilde H^n(\bigvee X_\alpha)\to\prod\tilde H^n(X_\alpha)$ is an isomorphism (for finitely many summands; the general case uses the same argument with the product axiom). It is a ring map because each $i_\alpha^*$ is. If $a$ restricts to zero on all summands but the $\alpha$-th and $b$ to zero on all but the $\beta$-th, with $\alpha\ne\beta$, then $ab$ restricts to zero on every summand, hence is $0$.

blocks.title: Cup-length
blocks.body:
(Contessoto et al., Definition 3.5.) The length $\mathrm{len}(A)$ of a graded ring $A$ is the largest $\ell$ such that there are homogeneous elements $a_1,\dots,a_\ell$ of positive degree with $a_1a_2\cdots a_\ell\ne0$ (and $0$ if all positive-degree products vanish, in particular if there are no positive-degree elements). The cup-length of a space is $\mathrm{cup}(X)=\mathrm{len}\,H^*(X;R)$ for a chosen coefficient ring, usually a field. It is a homotopy invariant, and it is a lower bound for the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of $X$, which is hard to compute. With field coefficients and spaces of finite type,
$$\mathrm{cup}(X\times Y)=\mathrm{cup}(X)+\mathrm{cup}(Y),\qquad\mathrm{cup}(X\sqcup Y)=\mathrm{cup}(X\vee Y)=\max\{\mathrm{cup}(X),\mathrm{cup}(Y)\}.$$
(Contessoto et al., Propositions 3.8 and 3.11; the printed formula for products has $\mathrm{len}(Y)$ for $\mathrm{cup}(Y)$, a typo, as their proof shows.) Wawrykow uses a relative of this invariant, the zero-divisor cup-length, as a lower bound for topological complexity; that is not developed here.

blocks.title: Torus versus wedge, by cup-length
blocks.body: Compute the cup-length, with coefficients in a field $F$, of $T^2$, $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$, $T^n$, $S^2\times S^4$, $S^1\sqcup T^3$, and $(S^1\vee S^1)\times S^1$.

blocks.body:
- The Künneth isomorphism needs hypotheses. With $\mathbb{Z}$ coefficients and torsion in $H^*(Y;\mathbb{Z})$ it can fail: for $X=Y=\mathbb{RP}^2$ the tensor product $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})^{\otimes2}$ is $\mathbb{Z},0,(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2,0,\mathbb{Z}/2$, but $H^3(\mathbb{RP}^2\times\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not hit; the general Künneth formula has an extra Tor term (Hatcher §3.B). Over a field there is no such problem for spaces of finite type.
- Hatcher's Exercise 3.2.10: for infinite discrete $X$ and $Y$ the cross product is not onto even in degree $0$, since $\prod_{\mathbb{N}}R\otimes\prod_{\mathbb{N}}R\to\prod_{\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}}R$ is not surjective. Finite generation is a real hypothesis.
- Papers often apply Künneth to cohomology rings without restating the hypotheses (field coefficients, finite type); check them before reusing a formula with integer coefficients.
- Graded tensor products carry the sign $(-1)^{|b||c|}$. Forgetting it gives a commutative ring instead of the exterior algebra for $T^n$.

items.q: Compute the ring $H^*(S^2\times S^2;\mathbb{Z})$ and show that it is not isomorphic to $H^*(S^2\vee S^2\vee S^4;\mathbb{Z})$.
items.hint: Look at the cup product pairing $H^2\times H^2\to H^4$.
items.solution: Basis $1,a,b,ab$ with $|a|=|b|=2$, $a^2=b^2=0$, $ab=ba$ generating $H^4$. The pairing $H^2\times H^2\to H^4\cong\mathbb{Z}$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, nonzero. In the wedge every product of two degree-$2$ classes is $0$ (they restrict to the two $S^2$ summands). A ring isomorphism would preserve the property 'some product $H^2\times H^2\to H^4$ is nonzero'.

items.q: Give the Poincaré series $\sum_k\dim H^k(-;\mathbb{Q})\,t^k$ of $T^3$, $S^1\times S^2$, $S^2\times S^2\times S^2$, and check $P_{X\times Y}=P_XP_Y$.
items.hint: Künneth over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives dimensions as a product.
items.solution: $P_{S^1}=1+t$, $P_{S^2}=1+t^2$. $P_{T^3}=(1+t)^3=1+3t+3t^2+t^3$; $P_{S^1\times S^2}=(1+t)(1+t^2)=1+t+t^2+t^3$; $P_{(S^2)^3}=(1+t^2)^3=1+3t^2+3t^4+t^6$. Künneth over a field gives $H^n(X\times Y)\cong\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^i(X)\otimes H^j(Y)$, hence $P_{X\times Y}=P_XP_Y$.

items.q: Compute the ring $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2\times\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ (granting $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[x]/(x^3)$, proved in the next section) and its cup-length.
items.hint: Künneth over the field $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
items.solution: $H^*\cong\mathbb{Z}/2[x_1,x_2]/(x_1^3,x_2^3)$ with $x_i=p_i^*x$ (signs are irrelevant mod $2$). Dimensions $1,2,3,2,1$ in degrees $0,\dots,4$. The product $x_1x_1x_2x_2=x_1^2x_2^2\ne0$ spans $H^4$, so the cup-length is $4=2+2$.

items.q:
Show that cross product with the generator $\theta\in H^1(S^1;\mathbb{Z})$ gives an isomorphism
$$H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})\oplus H^{n-1}(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong H^n(X\times S^1;\mathbb{Z}),$$
$(a,b)\mapsto a\times1+b\times\theta$, for every CW complex $X$.
items.hint: Apply Künneth with $Y=S^1$, whose cohomology is free of finite rank.
items.solution:
$H^*(S^1;\mathbb{Z})$ is free with basis $1,\theta$, so Künneth gives
$$\begin{aligned}H^n(X\times S^1)&\cong H^n(X)\otimes H^0(S^1)\oplus H^{n-1}(X)\otimes H^1(S^1)\\&=H^n(X)\otimes\mathbb{Z}\oplus H^{n-1}(X)\otimes\mathbb{Z}\theta\end{aligned},$$
with the map $a\otimes1+b\otimes\theta\mapsto a\times1+b\times\theta$. No hypothesis on $X$ beyond CW is needed, because the hypothesis is on the factor $Y=S^1$.

items.q: Verify the first pitfall: compute $H^3(\mathbb{RP}^2\times\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$ from the cellular chain complex of the product (the tensor product of the cellular complexes $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$), and show that the integral cross product is not onto in degree $3$.
items.hint: The product complex has ranks $1,2,3,2,1$. Compute $H_2$ and $H_3$, then use the universal coefficient theorem.
items.solution:
Write $e_0,e_1,e_2$ for the cells of $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $\partial e_1=0$, $\partial e_2=2e_1$, and use $\partial(u\otimes v)=\partial u\otimes v+(-1)^{|u|}u\otimes\partial v$. Degree $4$: $\partial(e_2e_2)=2e_1e_2+2e_2e_1$. Degree $3$: $\partial(e_1e_2)=-2e_1e_1$, $\partial(e_2e_1)=2e_1e_1$. Degree $2$: $\partial(e_0e_2)=2e_0e_1$, $\partial(e_2e_0)=2e_1e_0$, $\partial(e_1e_1)=0$. So $H_4=0$; $\ker\partial_3$ is spanned by $e_1e_2+e_2e_1$, and $\operatorname{im}\partial_4=2(e_1e_2+e_2e_1)$, so $H_3=\mathbb{Z}/2$; $\ker\partial_2=\mathbb{Z}e_1e_1$ and $\operatorname{im}\partial_3=2\mathbb{Z}e_1e_1$, so $H_2=\mathbb{Z}/2$; $H_1=(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, $H_0=\mathbb{Z}$. Universal coefficients:
$$\begin{aligned}H^3(\mathbb{RP}^2\times\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})&=\mathrm{Hom}(H_3,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(H_2,\mathbb{Z})\\&=\mathbb{Z}/2\end{aligned}.$$
But $\bigoplus_{i+j=3}H^i(\mathbb{RP}^2)\otimes H^j(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$, because $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=H^3(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=0$. So $\mu$ misses $H^3$.

blocks.body:
- $a\times b=p_1^*a\smile p_2^*b$; $(a\times b)(c\times d)=(-1)^{|b||c|}(ac)\times(bd)$; $a\smile b=\Delta^*(a\times b)$.
- Künneth: $H^*(X;R)\otimes_RH^*(Y;R)\cong H^*(X\times Y;R)$ as rings for CW complexes when $H^k(Y;R)$ is finitely generated free (always for fields and finite type).
- $H^*(T^n)=\Lambda[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$; $\tilde H^*$ of a wedge is the product ring; disjoint unions give products.
- Cup-length adds over products and takes the maximum over wedges; it separates $T^2$ (2) from $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2$ (1).

blocks.title: Projective spaces
blocks.body:
After this section you can use the rings of real and complex projective spaces, the most frequently quoted cohomology rings, and the standard arguments built on them: $\mathbb{CP}^2\not\simeq S^2\vee S^4$, the Hopf map is essential, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carries a division algebra structure only if $n$ is a power of $2$.

The groups are known from cells: $H^k(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$ for $0\le k\le n$, and $H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$ for $0\le k\le n$ with zero odd groups (all cellular boundaries vanish, as there are no cells in adjacent dimensions). The question is how the generators multiply.

blocks.title: Cohomology rings of projective spaces
blocks.body:
(Hatcher, Theorem 3.19 in the online version of §3.2.)
$$H^*(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2[a]/(a^{n+1}),\quad|a|=1;\qquad H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2[a];$$
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[b]/(b^{n+1}),\quad|b|=2;\qquad H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[b].$$
The quaternionic projective spaces satisfy $H^*(\mathbb{HP}^n;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[c]/(c^{n+1})$ with $|c|=4$, by the same proof. With integer coefficients, $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[x]/(2x)$ with $|x|=2$ (Hatcher §3.2, stated there after the theorem).

We follow Hatcher. Write $P^n=\mathbb{RP}^n$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients throughout; the complex case is identical with $\mathbb{C}$ for $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ for $\mathbb{Z}/2$, degrees doubled, and 'generator' for 'nonzero'.

Step 1 (reduction). Points of $P^n$ are lines $[x_0:\cdots:x_n]$. The subspace $P^{n-1}=\{x_n=0\}$ is the $(n-1)$-skeleton. Since all mod $2$ cellular coboundaries vanish, restriction $H^k(P^n)\to H^k(P^{n-1})$ is the projection of cellular cochains, an isomorphism for $k\le n-1$ (cellular cohomology theorem); more generally $H^k(P^n)\to H^k(P^m)$ is an isomorphism for $k\le m\le n$. By induction on $n$, assume $H^*(P^{n-1})=\mathbb{Z}/2[a]/(a^n)$. Restriction is a ring isomorphism in degrees $\le n-1$, so $a^k$ generates $H^k(P^n)$ for $k<n$, and it remains to show $a^n\ne0$. It suffices to prove: for $i+j=n$, the product of the generators of $H^i(P^n)$ and $H^j(P^n)$ is the generator of $H^n(P^n)$. (Take $i=n-1$, $j=1$.) We may assume $i,j\ge1$.

Step 2 (geometry). Let $P^i=\{x_{i+1}=\cdots=x_n=0\}$ and $P^j=\{x_0=\cdots=x_{i-1}=0\}$; they are copies of $\mathbb{RP}^i$ and $\mathbb{RP}^j$ meeting in the single point $p=[0:\cdots:0:1:0:\cdots:0]$ (only $x_i\ne0$). Let $U=\{x_i\ne0\}$. Normalising $x_i=1$ identifies $U$ with $\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^i\times\mathbb{R}^j$, the coordinates $(x_0,\dots,x_{i-1})$ and $(x_{i+1},\dots,x_n)$, with $p=0$, $P^i\cap U=\mathbb{R}^i\times0$, $P^j\cap U=0\times\mathbb{R}^j$.

Step 3 (the diagram). Consider the commutative diagram of cup products drawn below: the top row is $H^i(P^n)\times H^j(P^n)\to H^n(P^n)$; the middle row is the relative product
$$H^i(P^n,P^n\setminus P^j)\times H^j(P^n,P^n\setminus P^i)\to H^n(P^n,P^n\setminus p),$$
which lands there because $(P^n\setminus P^j)\cup(P^n\setminus P^i)=P^n\setminus p$ and the two subsets are open; the bottom row is the same product for $U$. The vertical maps forget the relative condition (up) or restrict to $U$ (down); naturality of relative cup products makes the squares commute. We show all vertical maps are isomorphisms and the bottom row sends generators to a generator.

Step 4 (right column). $P^n\setminus p$ deformation retracts onto $\{x_i=0\}\cong P^{n-1}$ by $t\mapsto[x_0:\cdots:tx_i:\cdots:x_n]$, which never passes through $p$. In the long exact sequence of $(P^n,P^n\setminus p)$, $H^{n-1}(P^n)\to H^{n-1}(P^n\setminus p)\cong H^{n-1}(P^{n-1})$ is onto (Step 1) and $H^n(P^{n-1})=0$, so $H^n(P^n,P^n\setminus p)\to H^n(P^n)$ is an isomorphism. Restriction $H^n(P^n,P^n\setminus p)\to H^n(U,U\setminus p)$ is an isomorphism by excision of the closed set $\{x_i=0\}$, which lies in the open set $P^n\setminus p$.

Step 5 (left column). $P^n\setminus P^j$ consists of the points with some $x_0,\dots,x_{i-1}$ nonzero; scaling $x_i,\dots,x_n$ by $t\to0$ deformation retracts it onto $P^{i-1}=\{x_i=\cdots=x_n=0\}$. In the long exact sequence of $(P^n,P^n\setminus P^j)$, $H^{i-1}(P^n)\to H^{i-1}(P^{i-1})$ is onto and $H^i(P^{i-1})=0$, so $H^i(P^n,P^n\setminus P^j)\to H^i(P^n)$ is an isomorphism. For the restriction to $U$, compare both pairs with $(P^i,P^i\setminus p)$ and $(\mathbb{R}^i,\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)=(P^i\cap U,P^i\cap U\setminus p)$:
- $H^i(P^n,P^n\setminus P^j)\to H^i(P^i,P^i\setminus p)$ is an isomorphism, by the five lemma applied to the two long exact sequences, since $H^k(P^n)\to H^k(P^i)$ is an isomorphism for $k\le i$ and both $P^n\setminus P^j$ and $P^i\setminus p$ deformation retract compatibly onto $P^{i-1}$;
- $H^i(P^i,P^i\setminus p)\to H^i(P^i\cap U,P^i\cap U\setminus p)$ is an isomorphism by excision of $P^{i-1}$;
- $H^i(U,U\setminus P^j)\to H^i(\mathbb{R}^i\times0,(\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)\times0)$ is an isomorphism, because $(\mathbb{R}^i\times\mathbb{R}^j,(\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)\times\mathbb{R}^j)$ deformation retracts onto $(\mathbb{R}^i\times0,(\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)\times0)$.
The square formed by these restrictions commutes, so $H^i(P^n,P^n\setminus P^j)\to H^i(U,U\setminus P^j)$ is an isomorphism. The same holds with $i$ and $j$ exchanged.

Step 6 (bottom row). Under $U=\mathbb{R}^i\times\mathbb{R}^j$, with $U\setminus P^j=(\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)\times\mathbb{R}^j$ and $U\setminus P^i=\mathbb{R}^i\times(\mathbb{R}^j\setminus0)$, the bottom product is the relative cross product
$$H^i(\mathbb{R}^i,\mathbb{R}^i\setminus0)\times H^j(\mathbb{R}^j,\mathbb{R}^j\setminus0)\to H^n(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}^n\setminus0).$$
These pairs are homotopy equivalent to $(D^i,\partial D^i)$, etc., and by the relative Künneth theorem the cross product of generators is a generator.

Step 7 (conclusion). Going up the left column, the generators of $H^i(U,U\setminus P^j)$ and $H^j(U,U\setminus P^i)$ correspond to the generators of $H^i(P^n)$ and $H^j(P^n)$; their product corresponds, going up the right column, to the generator of $H^n(P^n)$. So $a^ia^j=a^n$ generates $H^n(P^n)$.

Infinite case. $H^k(P^\infty)\to H^k(P^n)$ is an isomorphism for $k\le n$ (cellular cochains again), and it is a ring map, so no power of $a$ vanishes: $H^*(P^\infty)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a]$. Likewise for $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$.

All vertical maps are isomorphisms, and the bottom row is the relative cross product of discs, which sends generators to a generator.

blocks.title: CP^2 is not S^2 v S^4, and the Hopf map is essential
blocks.body:
(a) Show that $\mathbb{CP}^2$ and $S^2\vee S^4$ have isomorphic cohomology groups but are not homotopy equivalent.

(b) The Hopf map $\eta\colon S^3\to S^2=\mathbb{CP}^1$, $x\mapsto[\mathbb{C}x]$ (the complex line through $x\in S^3\subset\mathbb{C}^2$), has mapping cone $C_\eta=D^4\cup_\eta S^2\cong\mathbb{CP}^2$. Deduce that $\eta$ is not null-homotopic.
blocks.solution:
(a) Both have $H^0=H^2=H^4=\mathbb{Z}$ and zero otherwise. In $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^2)=\mathbb{Z}[b]/(b^3)$ the square of the generator $b\in H^2$ generates $H^4$. In $S^2\vee S^4$ the generator $s\in H^2$ restricts to $0$ on $S^4$ and to the generator of $H^2(S^2)$, so $s^2$ restricts to $0$ on $S^4$ (degree) and to $0$ on $S^2$ ($H^4(S^2)=0$); by the wedge theorem $s^2=0$. A homotopy equivalence would induce a ring isomorphism carrying $b$ to $\pm s$ and $b^2$ to $s^2=0$, impossible.

(b) If $\eta$ were null-homotopic, its mapping cone would be homotopy equivalent to the cone on a constant map, $C_\eta\simeq S^4\vee S^2$ (Quick, Lecture 21: the mapping cone of a null-homotopic $f\colon X\to Y$ is $\simeq\Sigma X\vee Y$, and $\Sigma S^3=S^4$). But $C_\eta\cong\mathbb{CP}^2\not\simeq S^2\vee S^4$ by (a). So $[\eta]\neq0$ in $\pi_3(S^2)$. The quaternionic Hopf map $S^7\to S^4$ is treated the same way with $\mathbb{HP}^2$.

blocks.title: Division algebras exist only in dimensions 2^r
blocks.body: Suppose $\mu\colon\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is bilinear without zero divisors ($\mu(x,y)=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$). Show that $n$ is a power of $2$.
blocks.solution:
Step 1 (a map of projective spaces). Bilinearity and the absence of zero divisors give a well-defined map $h\colon\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}\to\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$, $h([x],[y])=[\mu(x,y)]$, since $\mu(sx,ty)=st\,\mu(x,y)$ and $\mu(x,y)\neq0$.

Step 2 (its effect on $H^1$). By Künneth over $\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{RP}^{n-1};\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a_1,a_2]/(a_1^n,a_2^n)$ with $a_i=p_i^*a$. So $h^*(a)=\lambda_1a_1+\lambda_2a_2$. Fix $y_0\neq0$; the map $x\mapsto\mu(x,y_0)$ is linear and injective, hence an isomorphism, so $[x]\mapsto h([x],[y_0])$ is a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ and acts as the identity on $H^1$. Restricting $h^*(a)$ to $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}\times[y_0]$ kills $a_2$ and gives $\lambda_1a$; so $\lambda_1=1$. Similarly $\lambda_2=1$, and $h^*(a)=a_1+a_2$.

Step 3 (the binomial obstruction). $a^n=0$ in $H^n(\mathbb{RP}^{n-1})$, so
$$0=h^*(a^n)=(a_1+a_2)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_1^ka_2^{n-k}=\sum_{0<k<n}\binom nk a_1^ka_2^{n-k},$$
using $a_1^n=a_2^n=0$. The monomials $a_1^ka_2^{n-k}$, $0<k<n$, are linearly independent, so $\binom nk$ is even for all $0<k<n$, i.e. $(1+x)^n=1+x^n$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$.

Step 4 (only powers of 2). Write $n=2^rm$ with $m$ odd. In $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$, squaring is additive, so $(1+x)^n=\big((1+x)^{2^r}\big)^m=(1+x^{2^r})^m$, which contains the term $m\,x^{2^r}=x^{2^r}$. If $m>1$ then $0<2^r<n$, and this term contradicts Step 3. So $m=1$ and $n=2^r$. (The real division algebras $\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H},\mathbb{O}$ have $n=1,2,4,8$; that no others exist needs more than cohomology.)

items.q: What is the cup-length of $\mathbb{RP}^n$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients, and of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with $\mathbb{Z}$ coefficients?
items.a: $n$ in both cases: $a^n\neq0$ (respectively $b^n\neq0$), and any product of more than $n$ positive-degree classes lies above the top dimension.

items.q: Why can $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ have $a^2\neq0$ with $|a|=1$ without contradicting graded commutativity?
items.a: Graded commutativity only gives $2a^2=0$, which is automatic mod $2$.

items.q: Is $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$ isomorphic as a ring to $H^*(S^2\times S^2;\mathbb{Z})$?
items.a: No; the groups already differ ($H^2$ has rank $1$ versus $2$).

items.q: Decide whether $\mathbb{CP}^3$ and $S^2\times S^4$ are homotopy equivalent.
items.hint: Compare the groups, then the rings.
items.solution: The groups agree ($\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0,2,4,6$). In $\mathbb{CP}^3$ the square of the degree-$2$ generator generates $H^4$. In $S^2\times S^4$ the degree-$2$ generator $a=x\times1$ satisfies $a^2=x^2\times1=0$. So the rings differ and the spaces are not homotopy equivalent.

items.q: Compute $(a_1+a_2)^4$ in $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty\times\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a_1,a_2]$, and $(a_1+a_2)^3$.
items.hint: Binomial coefficients mod $2$.

items.q: Show that for $m>n$ there is no map $f\colon\mathbb{RP}^m\to\mathbb{RP}^n$ with $f^*\neq0$ on $H^1(-;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
items.hint: Compare $f^*(a^{n+1})$ with $(f^*a)^{n+1}$.
items.solution: If $f^*(a)\neq0$ then $f^*(a)=a'$, the generator of $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^m;\mathbb{Z}/2)$. Then $a'^{n+1}=f^*(a^{n+1})=f^*(0)=0$. But $n+1\le m$, so $a'^{n+1}\neq0$ in $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^m;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a']/(a'^{m+1})$. Contradiction. (This is the cohomological core of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem.)

items.q: Show that every map $f\colon\mathbb{CP}^n\to\mathbb{CP}^n$ with $f^*(b)=d\,b$ has $f^*$ equal to multiplication by $d^k$ on $H^{2k}$, and that the Lefschetz number $\sum_k(-1)^k\operatorname{tr}(f^*|H^k(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb{Q}))$ equals $1+d+\cdots+d^n$.
items.hint: $f^*$ is a ring homomorphism.
items.solution:
$f^*(b^k)=(f^*b)^k=d^kb^k$, and $b^k$ generates $H^{2k}$. All odd groups vanish, so the alternating sum of traces is $\sum_{k=0}^nd^k$. (Granting the Lefschetz fixed point theorem, which is not proved on this page: for $n$ even this number is never $0$ for integer $d$, since for $d
eq1$ it equals $(d^{n+1}-1)/(d-1)$ and $d^{n+1}
eq1$ for $d
eq\pm1$, while $d=-1$ gives $1$; so every self-map of $\mathbb{CP}^{2m}$ has a fixed point.)

items.q: Prove $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[b]$ and $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2[a]$ from the finite cases, carefully justifying why no relation $b^N=0$ can hold.
items.hint: Restriction to the finite skeleta is a ring homomorphism and an isomorphism in low degrees.
items.solution: $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$ is a CW complex with one cell in each even dimension, $\mathbb{CP}^N$ its $2N$-skeleton, and all cellular coboundaries are zero. Hence $H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)=\mathbb{Z}$ for all $k$, odd groups vanish, and restriction $r_N\colon H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)\to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N)$ is an isomorphism in degrees $\le2N$. Let $b$ generate $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)$. For each $k$ choose $N\ge k$: $r_N(b^k)=r_N(b)^k$ generates $H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^N)$ by the finite theorem, and $r_N$ is an isomorphism in degree $2k$, so $b^k$ generates $H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)$. Thus $\mathbb{Z}[b]\to H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)$ is an isomorphism in every degree; in particular $b^N\ne0$ for all $N$. The real case is the same with $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

blocks.body:
- $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a]/(a^{n+1})$, $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[b]/(b^{n+1})$; infinite versions are polynomial; $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^\infty;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[x]/(2x)$, $|x|=2$.
- Proof: the product of generators in complementary degrees is a generator, by localising at the point $P^i\cap P^j$ and the relative Künneth theorem.
- Uses: $\mathbb{CP}^2\not\simeq S^2\vee S^4$, the Hopf map is essential, division algebras only in dimensions $2^r$, no map $\mathbb{RP}^m\to\mathbb{RP}^n$ ($m>n$) nonzero on $H^1$.

blocks.title: Degree one: classes as maps to the circle
blocks.body:
After this section you can pass between integral degree-one classes and maps to the circle, in both directions, which is how circular coordinates in data analysis are built and how papers use $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})$ without naming it.

A map $f\colon X\to S^1$ pulls back the generator of $H^1(S^1;\mathbb{Z})$ to a class $f^*\Theta\in H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})$, which records how many times $f$ winds each loop of $X$ around the circle. The question is whether every class arises this way, and whether the class determines $f$ up to homotopy. Here $\Theta$ denotes the generator of $H^1(S^1;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(S^1),\mathbb{Z})$ taking the value $1$ on the class of the loop $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$.

blocks.title: Maps to the circle
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a connected CW complex. Then
$$[X,S^1]\to H^1(X;\mathbb{Z}),\qquad[f]\mapsto f^*\Theta,$$
is a bijection from free homotopy classes of maps to the circle onto the first integral cohomology group. It is a group isomorphism when $[X,S^1]$ is given the group structure of pointwise multiplication of maps into $S^1\subset\mathbb{C}$. Under $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X,x_0),\mathbb{Z})$ the class $f^*\Theta$ corresponds to the homomorphism $\gamma\mapsto\deg(f\circ\gamma)$.

More generally (Wikipedia, Eilenberg–MacLane space): for a based CW complex $X$, reduced $\tilde H^n(X;G)$ is naturally isomorphic to the group of based homotopy classes $[X,K(G,n)]_*$, via pullback of a fundamental class, where $K(G,n)$ is a space with $\pi_n=G$ and all other homotopy groups trivial. Examples: $K(\mathbb{Z},1)=S^1$, $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)=\mathbb{RP}^\infty$, $K(\mathbb{Z},2)=\mathbb{CP}^\infty$. This general statement is not proved here; it belongs with [[homotopy-groups]].

Idea: identify both sides with $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X),\mathbb{Z})$; injectivity is the lifting criterion for the covering $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ (Schultz), surjectivity is a construction cell by cell.

The identification. By the universal coefficient theorem and Hurewicz,
$$\begin{aligned}H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})&\cong\mathrm{Hom}(H_1(X),\mathbb{Z})\\&\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X,x_0),\mathbb{Z})\end{aligned},$$
and $f^*\Theta$ goes to $[\gamma]\mapsto\langle f^*\Theta,[\gamma]\rangle=\langle\Theta,[f\circ\gamma]\rangle=\deg(f\circ\gamma)$, the degree of the loop $f\circ\gamma$ in $S^1$, defined by lifting to $\mathbb{R}$ as on [[fundamental-group]].

Homomorphism. If $f\circ\gamma=e^{2\pi iu}$ and $g\circ\gamma=e^{2\pi iv}$ with lifts $u,v\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$, then $(fg)\circ\gamma=e^{2\pi i(u+v)}$, so $\deg((fg)\circ\gamma)=\deg(f\circ\gamma)+\deg(g\circ\gamma)$. Pointwise multiplication is compatible with homotopy, so $[X,S^1]$ is a group and the map is a homomorphism (Schultz, steps 1-2).

Injective. Suppose $f^*\Theta=0$. Choose a path from $f(x_0)$ to $1$ and rotate: $f$ is homotopic to $f_b=f\cdot f(x_0)^{-1}$, which sends $x_0$ to $1$, with the same class. Then $(f_b)_*\colon\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\pi_1(S^1,1)$ is zero, so by the lifting criterion of [[covering-spaces]] ($X$ is connected and locally path connected) $f_b=\exp(2\pi iF)$ for some $F\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$. Then $\exp(2\pi itF)$, $t\in[0,1]$, is a homotopy from the constant map to $f_b$. So the kernel is trivial; being a homomorphism, the map is injective.

Surjective. Let $h\colon\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb{Z}$ be a homomorphism. Choose a maximal tree $T$ in the $1$-skeleton $X^1$ and send $T$ to $1\in S^1$. Each edge $e\not\subset T$ closes up through $T$ to a loop $\gamma_e$, and these loops freely generate $\pi_1(X^1,x_0)$; map $e$ around the circle $h(\bar\gamma_e)$ times, where $\bar\gamma_e$ is the image of $\gamma_e$ in $\pi_1(X)$. The resulting $f_1\colon X^1\to S^1$ satisfies $\deg(f_1\circ\gamma)=h(\bar\gamma)$ for every loop in $X^1$, since both sides are homomorphisms that agree on generators. A $2$-cell is attached along a loop $\varphi$ that is null-homotopic in $X$, so $h(\bar\varphi)=0$: $f_1\circ\varphi$ has degree $0$, is null-homotopic, and $f_1$ extends over the cell. For a $k$-cell with $k\ge3$ the attaching map comes from $S^{k-1}$, which is simply connected, so $f\circ\varphi$ lifts to $\mathbb{R}$ and is null-homotopic; $f$ extends again. Proceeding cell by cell gives $f\colon X\to S^1$, and since $\pi_1(X^1)\to\pi_1(X)$ is onto, $f_*=h$. Schultz proves injectivity and states surjectivity for cell complexes; the extension argument is the degree-one case of the obstruction-theoretic proof of representability.

blocks.title: Circular coordinates on a triangle
blocks.body:
Scoccola et al. turn an integral $1$-cocycle on a simplicial complex $K$ into a circle-valued function on the vertices: replace it by a cohomologous real cocycle $\theta$ (in their Algorithm 3, the harmonic representative, the one of least norm), fix a base vertex $x$, and set
$$f(y)=\theta^{y_0y_1}+\theta^{y_1y_2}+\cdots+\theta^{y_{\ell-1}y_\ell}\pmod{\mathbb{Z}}$$
for any edge path $x=y_0,\dots,y_\ell=y$ (their Algorithm 5; $\theta^{ji}=-\theta^{ij}$). Carry this out on the hollow triangle for the integral cocycle $[0,1]^*$, with base vertex $0$.
blocks.solution:
Well defined. Two edge paths from $x$ to $y$ differ by a closed edge path, and the sum of $\theta$ round a closed path equals the sum of the integral cocycle round it (they differ by a coboundary, whose sum round a loop telescopes to $0$), an integer. So $f(y)$ is well defined mod $\mathbb{Z}$.

The harmonic representative. Write $\theta=[0,1]^*-\delta\tau$ for a function $\tau$ on the vertices. On the edges $[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]$ this is $(1-(\tau_1-\tau_0),\ -(\tau_2-\tau_1),\ -(\tau_2-\tau_0))$. Minimising the sum of squares over $\tau$ (only differences matter, so put $\tau_0=0$) gives the critical point $\tau_1=2/3$, $\tau_2=1/3$, and
$$\theta=\big(\theta^{01},\theta^{12},\theta^{02}\big)=\big(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,-\tfrac13\big).$$
Its sum round the loop is $\theta^{01}+\theta^{12}-\theta^{02}=1$, as for $[0,1]^*$: the class is unchanged and the winding is spread evenly.

Integration. $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=\theta^{01}=\tfrac13$, $f(2)=\theta^{01}+\theta^{12}=\tfrac23$; along the other path $f(2)=\theta^{02}=-\tfrac13\equiv\tfrac23$. The three vertices go to three equally spaced points of $S^1=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, and extending linearly over the edges (each edge $[i,j]$ covering an arc of length $\theta^{ij}$) gives a degree-one map from the triangle, a circle, to $S^1$, the map corresponding to the generator of $H^1$ under the theorem above.

items.q: Which classes in $H^1(T^2;\mathbb{Z})$ correspond to the two projections $T^2\to S^1$?
items.a: $p_1^*\Theta=\alpha$ and $p_2^*\Theta=\beta$, the generators of the exterior algebra; the map $(z,w)\mapsto z^mw^n$ corresponds to $m\alpha+n\beta$.

items.q: Why is every map $\mathbb{RP}^2\to S^1$ null-homotopic?
items.a: $H^1(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})=0$, and the theorem says the class determines the homotopy class.

items.q: Show that every map $S^n\to S^1$ with $n\ge2$ is null-homotopic, and that $[T^n,S^1]\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$.
items.hint: Compute $H^1$.
items.solution: $H^1(S^n;\mathbb{Z})=0$ for $n\ge2$, so the only class is $0$, the class of the constant map. $H^1(T^n;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}^n$ with basis $\alpha_i=p_i^*\Theta$, so $[T^n,S^1]\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$, represented by $(z_1,\dots,z_n)\mapsto z_1^{m_1}\cdots z_n^{m_n}$.

items.q: For the hollow square with vertices $0,1,2,3$ and edges $[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[0,3]$, find the harmonic representative of $[0,1]^*$ and the circular coordinate with base vertex $0$.
items.hint: By symmetry the winding is spread evenly over the four edges.
items.solution: The harmonic representative has value $\tfrac14$ on $[0,1],[1,2],[2,3]$ and $-\tfrac14$ on $[0,3]$ (its sum round the loop is $1$ and each vertex has zero net flow). Integrating: $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=\tfrac14$, $f(2)=\tfrac12$, $f(3)=\tfrac34$.

items.q: Let $X$ be a connected CW complex with $H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})=0$. Show that every map $X\to S^1$ lifts to $\mathbb{R}$.
items.hint: Combine the theorem with the homotopy lifting property.
items.solution: By the theorem $f$ is homotopic to a constant map, which lifts. A homotopy $H\colon X\times I\to S^1$ from the constant map to $f$ lifts to $\tilde H\colon X\times I\to\mathbb{R}$ starting at a constant lift, by the homotopy lifting property of the covering $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$; then $\tilde H(-,1)$ lifts $f$. (Alternatively: $H^1=0$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1X,\mathbb{Z})=0$, so $f_*=0$, and the lifting criterion applies.)

items.q: Let $K$ be a finite connected simplicial complex and $\theta$ a real $1$-cocycle whose class lies in the image of $H^1(K;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(K;\mathbb{R})$. Show that the circular coordinate $f$ of the example, extended linearly over edges, extends to a continuous map $|K|\to S^1$ whose class in $H^1(K;\mathbb{Z})$ maps to $[\theta]$.
items.hint: On each triangle the three edge arcs close up because $\theta$ is a cocycle; higher simplices are simply connected.
items.solution: On an edge $[i,j]$ map linearly onto the arc from $f(i)$ of signed length $\theta^{ij}$; this ends at $f(j)$ because $f(j)-f(i)\equiv\theta^{ij}$. On a triangle $[i,j,k]$ the boundary loop then has total signed length $\theta^{ij}+\theta^{jk}-\theta^{ik}=\delta\theta[i,j,k]=0$, so it has degree $0$ and the map extends over the triangle (lift to $\mathbb{R}$ and extend, for instance, linearly in barycentric coordinates). On a simplex of dimension $\ge3$ the boundary is a sphere $S^{k-1}$ with $k-1\ge2$, simply connected, so the map lifts to $\mathbb{R}$ there and extends. The resulting $f$ sends each edge loop $\gamma$ to a loop of degree $\sum_\gamma\theta$, so $f^*\Theta$ evaluates on $[\gamma]$ to $\langle\theta,\gamma\rangle$; by the universal coefficient theorem ($H^1=\mathrm{Hom}(H_1,-)$) $f^*\Theta$ maps to $[\theta]$ in $H^1(K;\mathbb{R})$.

blocks.body:
- $[X,S^1]\cong H^1(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1X,\mathbb{Z})$ for connected CW $X$, via $f\mapsto f^*\Theta$ and degrees of loops.
- Integral cocycles integrate to circle-valued coordinates; real representatives of integral classes (e.g. harmonic ones) give the same map up to homotopy.
- In general $\tilde H^n(X;G)=[X,K(G,n)]_*$, with $K(\mathbb{Z},1)=S^1$, $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)=\mathbb{RP}^\infty$, $K(\mathbb{Z},2)=\mathbb{CP}^\infty$.

blocks.title: Sign conventions
blocks.body:
After this section you can recognise which conventions a paper uses for the coboundary and the cup product, and convert formulas between them.

The groups $H^n(X;G)$ do not depend on these choices, and neither does the ring up to isomorphism, but explicit formulas do: signs in Leibniz rules, in commuting diagrams, and in intersection and linking forms. Conway, Friedl and Herrmann, who compute linking forms, warn that their signs should be 'taken with a grain of salt' after finding many sign errors, including their own.

blocks.title: Coboundary and cup product signs
blocks.body: Two independent choices: the sign of $\delta$, and the sign in the evaluation of a tensor product of cochains, which enters the cup product. Conventions that make evaluation a chain map (the Koszul convention) put signs in both.

rows.text: $\delta_n=\partial_{n+1}^*$, i.e. $(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\partial\sigma)$; $(\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)=\varphi(\text{front})\psi(\text{back})$ with no sign; Leibniz rule $\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile\psi+(-1)^k\varphi\smile\delta\psi$.
Same as Hatcher: $\delta(c)=c\circ\partial$ and the unsigned front-face/back-face product.
$\delta_n=(-1)^{n+1}\partial_{n+1}^*$. Conway–Friedl–Herrmann report that Bredon's cup product differs from Hatcher's by $(-1)^{kl}$ in degrees $k,l$, and his cap product by $(-1)^{k(l-k)}$.

$(df)(\sigma)=(-1)^{n+1}f(d\sigma)$ for $f$ of degree $n$, chosen so that the Kronecker pairing is a chain map; the evaluation of a tensor product of cochains carries the Koszul sign, $(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{pq}f(x)g(y)$, so the cochain cross and cup products contain $(-1)^{pq}$: $(f\smile g)(\sigma)=(-1)^{pq}f(\text{front})g(\text{back})$.

rows.who: Graded tensor products (all of the above)
rows.text: $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=(-1)^{|b||c|}ac\otimes bd$, and the cross product $H^*(X)\otimes H^*(Y)\to H^*(X\times Y)$ is a ring map for this rule (Hatcher §3.2; Miller, Proposition 29.2).

No signs at all: $\partial|0\cdots k\rangle=\sum_i|0\cdots\hat\imath\cdots k\rangle$, $\delta$ of an indicator cochain is the sum of its cofaces, and the cup product needs a branching structure (a local vertex order, equivalently arrows on edges without oriented triangles).

blocks.title: Converting between the two cup products
blocks.body: Let $\smile'$ be the cup product with the extra sign, $\varphi\smile'\psi=(-1)^{kl}\varphi\smile\psi$ for $|\varphi|=k$, $|\psi|=l$ (Miller's convention, and up to this sign Bredon's). Show that $a\mapsto\eta(a)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}a$ on $H^k$ is a ring isomorphism from $(H^*,\smile')$ to $(H^*,\smile)$, so the two conventions give isomorphic rings, and find the sign relating $\alpha\smile'\beta$ and $\alpha\smile\beta$ on the torus.
blocks.solution: We need $\eta(a\smile'b)=\eta(a)\smile\eta(b)$ for $|a|=k$, $|b|=l$. The left side is $(-1)^{(k+l)(k+l-1)/2}(-1)^{kl}a\smile b$ and the right side is $(-1)^{k(k-1)/2+l(l-1)/2}a\smile b$. Since $(k+l)(k+l-1)/2=k(k-1)/2+l(l-1)/2+kl$, the left exponent is $k(k-1)/2+l(l-1)/2+2kl$, which has the same parity as the right one. So $\eta$ is a ring isomorphism (it is bijective, being $\pm1$ in each degree). On the torus, $\alpha\smile'\beta=(-1)^{1\cdot1}\alpha\smile\beta=-\gamma$: the generator of $H^2$ called '$\alpha\beta$' in one convention is $-\alpha\beta$ in the other, which is exactly the kind of discrepancy that changes the sign of an intersection form.

blocks.body:
- Mixing conventions inside one computation (Hatcher's coboundary with a Koszul-signed cup product, say) breaks the Leibniz rule; fix one source's conventions and keep them.
- $\mathbb{Z}/2$ formulas from lattice papers hide all signs; lifting them to $\mathbb{Z}$ coefficients requires choosing orientations and conventions, and Chen and Tata note that integer versions of the higher cup products carry different sign conventions from Steenrod's.
- Explicit cocycle formulas depend on the vertex order (or branching structure). A cocycle written for one order is cohomologous, not equal, to the one for another order.
- When a paper says that two classes 'intersect with sign $-1$', check its convention for the cup product, for the orientation of the fundamental class and for the order of the factors before comparing with another paper.

items.q: In Miller's convention $(df)(\sigma)=(-1)^{n+1}f(d\sigma)$, compute $df$ for a $0$-cochain $f$ on a $1$-simplex $\sigma$ from $x$ to $y$, and compare with Hatcher's $\delta f$.
items.hint: Here $n=0$.
items.solution:
$$\begin{aligned}(df)(\sigma)&=(-1)^{1}f(\partial\sigma)\\&=-(f(y)-f(x))=f(x)-f(y)\end{aligned},$$
the negative of Hatcher's $(\delta f)(\sigma)=f(y)-f(x)$. The cocycles and coboundaries are the same subgroups, so $H^0$ and all $H^n$ agree.

items.q: Show that with Miller's signs the Leibniz rule still holds in the form $d(\varphi\smile'\psi)=d\varphi\smile'\psi+(-1)^k\varphi\smile'd\psi$, where $d=(-1)^{n+1}\delta$ on $C^n$ and $\varphi\smile'\psi=(-1)^{kl}\varphi\smile\psi$.
items.hint: Substitute and compare the signs of the three terms, using Hatcher's Leibniz rule.
items.solution:
Let $|\varphi|=k$, $|\psi|=l$. Left:
$$\begin{aligned}d(\varphi\smile'\psi)&=(-1)^{k+l+1}(-1)^{kl}\delta(\varphi\smile\psi)\\&=(-1)^{k+l+1+kl}\big(\delta\varphi\smile\psi\\&\qquad+(-1)^k\varphi\smile\delta\psi\big)\end{aligned}.$$
First term on the right:
$$\begin{aligned}d\varphi\smile'\psi&=(-1)^{(k+1)l}(-1)^{k+1}\delta\varphi\smile\psi\\&=(-1)^{kl+l+k+1}\delta\varphi\smile\psi\end{aligned},$$
matching. Second:
$$\begin{aligned}(-1)^k\varphi\smile'd\psi&=(-1)^k(-1)^{k(l+1)}(-1)^{l+1}\varphi\smile\delta\psi\\&=(-1)^{kl+l+1}\varphi\smile\delta\psi\end{aligned}$$
(as $(-1)^{2k}=1$), and on the left the coefficient is $(-1)^{k+l+1+kl+k}=(-1)^{kl+l+1}$, matching.

- Hatcher, Munkres, Quick: $\delta=\partial^*$, unsigned cup product; Bredon and Miller: $\delta=(-1)^{n+1}\partial^*$, and cup products differing by $(-1)^{kl}$.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Here is where each paper's prerequisites from this page are treated, and what they need from elsewhere.

1. Contessoto, Mémoli, Stefanou and Zhou, persistent cup-length. Simplicial cochains over a field, cocycles and representatives (Cochains on a simplicial complex); the cup product on an ordered simplicial complex by concatenation and the cohomology ring as a functor (The cup product); cup-length and its behaviour under products, disjoint unions and wedges, and the torus versus $S^1\vee S^2\vee S^1$ (Products of spaces); the Klein bottle mod $2$ and $\Lambda[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d]$ for $T^d$ (The cup product; Products of spaces). Persistence itself is a separate topic.
2. Chen and Tata, higher cup products on hypercubic lattices. $\mathbb{Z}/2$ cochains as functions on simplices, $\delta$ as the sum over cofaces, the branching structure, the Leibniz rule mod $2$ (Cochains; The cup product; Sign conventions), and the cup-1 product with $\delta(\alpha\smile_1\beta)=\alpha\smile\beta+\beta\smile\alpha$ (Graded commutativity). Cubical cochains, higher cup-$i$ products and the dual-cellulation picture of Poincaré duality are beyond this page.
3. Scoccola et al., toroidal coordinates. Integer and real $1$-cocycles, $H^1=Z^1/\operatorname{im}\delta$, the change of coefficients $H^1(B;\mathbb{Z})\to H^1(B;\mathbb{R})$ and its lattice of integral classes (Universal coefficients), and integration of cocycles to circle-valued maps (Degree one). Harmonic representatives with respect to an inner product are their own linear algebra; the smooth version, de Rham classes with integral periods, is on [[de-rham-cohomology]].
4. Wawrykow, topological complexity of configuration spaces of disks. Künneth isomorphism and cross product, graded commutativity to reorder products, vanishing above the dimension of a CW model (Products of spaces; Graded commutativity). Zero-divisors and Farber's bound, and Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, are not covered here.
5. Bastl et al., algorithms in $4$-manifold topology. Relative cohomology, universal coefficients over $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$, Mayer–Vietoris (Singular cohomology; Universal coefficients). The fundamental class, Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, the intersection form and its signature, and the Wu formula are on the separate pages on Poincaré duality and cohomology operations.
6. The paper on $p$-primary subgroups of $H^*(BPU_n)$. Integral cohomology rings, polynomial rings such as $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)=\mathbb{Z}[b]$ (Projective spaces), cup product manipulations and Künneth for free factors (Products of spaces). The rings $H^*(BU_n)=\mathbb{Z}[c_1,\dots,c_n]$, $H^*(BT^n)$, Eilenberg–MacLane spaces $K(\mathbb{Z},3)$ and the multiplicative Serre spectral sequence belong to characteristic classes and [[spectral-sequences]].

This page dualises [[homology]] using [[homological-algebra]] (exactness, five lemma, long exact sequences) and [[ext]] (the universal coefficient theorem). With real coefficients on a smooth manifold, [[de-rham-cohomology]] computes the same ring by closed forms, with the wedge product as cup product, and [[poincare-duality]] gives the de Rham form of duality. The topological Poincaré duality theorem, $H^k(M;R)\cong H_{n-k}(M;R)$ for a closed $R$-oriented $n$-manifold by cap product with a fundamental class, is the next step and needs a page of its own: orientations, fundamental classes and the cap product $H_n\times H^k\to H_{n-k}$. Representability $\tilde H^n(X;G)=[X,K(G,n)]_*$ connects cohomology to [[homotopy-groups]] and makes cohomology operations such as Steenrod squares maps between Eilenberg–MacLane spaces; the cup-1 product above is their cochain-level origin. Multiplicative [[spectral-sequences]] compute cohomology rings of fibrations from those of base and fibre, and [[k-theory]] is a generalised cohomology theory that keeps the axioms of this page but replaces the dimension axiom. [[sheaf-cohomology]] and [[galois-cohomology]] use the same word for derived functors in other settings, and lifting maps to the circle uses [[covering-spaces]].

import itertools, random
from fractions import Fraction
from sympy import Matrix, ZZ
from sympy.matrices.normalforms import smith_normal_form

def invariants(M):
    """nonzero invariant factors of an integer matrix (list of positive ints)"""
    if M.rows == 0 or M.cols == 0:
        return []
    S = smith_normal_form(M, domain=ZZ)
    return [abs(S[i, i]) for i in range(min(S.rows, S.cols)) if S[i, i] != 0]

def homology(dims, bd):
    """dims[n] = rank of C_n; bd[n] = matrix of d_n: C_n -> C_{n-1} (rows dims[n-1], cols dims[n]).
    returns list of (free rank, sorted torsion list) for H_n"""
    N = len(dims)
    out = []
    for n in range(N):
        dn = bd.get(n)
        r_out = len(invariants(dn)) if dn is not None else 0
        dn1 = bd.get(n + 1)
        inv_in = invariants(dn1) if dn1 is not None else []
        free = dims[n] - r_out - len(inv_in)
        tors = sorted(x for x in inv_in if x > 1)
        out.append((free, tors))
    return out

def cohomology_from_cochains(dims, bd):
    """cohomology of Hom(C,Z): coboundary delta_n = d_{n+1}^T : C^n -> C^{n+1}"""
    N = len(dims)
    cob = {}
    for n in range(N):
        if (n + 1) in bd:
            cob[n] = bd[n + 1].T
    out = []
    for n in range(N):
        dn = cob.get(n)
        r_out = len(invariants(dn)) if dn is not None else 0
        dprev = cob.get(n - 1)
        inv_in = invariants(dprev) if dprev is not None else []
        free = dims[n] - r_out - len(inv_in)
        tors = sorted(x for x in inv_in if x > 1)
        out.append((free, tors))
    return out

def rank_mod_p(M, p):
    M = [[int(x) % p for x in row] for row in M.tolist()]
    if not M or not M[0]:
        return 0
    rows, cols = len(M), len(M[0]); r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if M[i][c] % p), None)
        if piv is None: continue
        M[r], M[piv] = M[piv], M[r]
        inv = pow(M[r][c], -1, p)
        M[r] = [(x * inv) % p for x in M[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and M[i][c] % p:
                f = M[i][c]; M[i] = [(a - f * b) % p for a, b in zip(M[i], M[r])]
        r += 1
    return r

def simplicial_bd(simplices):
    """simplices: dict n -> sorted list of vertex tuples (closed under faces). returns dims, bd"""
    N = max(simplices) + 1
    idx = {n: {s: i for i, s in enumerate(simplices[n])} for n in simplices}
    dims = [len(simplices.get(n, [])) for n in range(N)]
    bd = {}
    for n in range(1, N):
        M = [[0] * dims[n] for _ in range(dims[n - 1])]
        for j, s in enumerate(simplices[n]):
            for i in range(n + 1):
                f = s[:i] + s[i + 1:]
                M[idx[n - 1][f]][j] += (-1) ** i
        bd[n] = Matrix(M)
    return dims, bd

def closure(maximal):
    S = {}
    for m in maximal:
        m = tuple(sorted(m))
        for k in range(1, len(m) + 1):
            for f in itertools.combinations(m, k):
                S.setdefault(k - 1, set()).add(f)
    return {n: sorted(S[n]) for n in S}


hollow = closure([(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)])
d, b = simplicial_bd(hollow)
assert cohomology_from_cochains(d, b) == [(1,[]),(1,[])]
filled = closure([(0,1,2)])
d, b = simplicial_bd(filled)
assert cohomology_from_cochains(d, b) == [(1,[]),(0,[]),(0,[])]
tet = closure([(0,1,2),(0,1,3),(0,2,3),(1,2,3)])
d, b = simplicial_bd(tet)
assert cohomology_from_cochains(d, b) == [(1,[]),(0,[]),(1,[])]
# fundamental cycle c = [123]-[023]+[013]-[012]
tri = tet[2]
c = [0]*len(tri)
for s, v in [((1,2,3),1),((0,2,3),-1),((0,1,3),1),((0,1,2),-1)]:
    c[tri.index(s)] = v
c = Matrix(c)
assert b[2] * c == Matrix([0]*len(tet[1]))
# image of delta_1 = b[2].T ; ev_c vanishes on it, and image + Z*[123]^* = Z^4 with index 1 kernel
D = b[2].T
assert (c.T * D) == Matrix([[0]*D.cols])
# kernel of ev_c is a saturated rank-3 sublattice; image of delta has invariant factors all 1
assert invariants(D) == [1,1,1]
# explicit procedure from the text for a random omega in ker ev_c
edges = tet[1]
for trial in range(50):
    w = {s: random.randint(-9,9) for s in tri}
    w[(1,2,3)] = w[(0,1,2)]*0 + random.randint(-9,9)
    # force ev_c(w)=0 by adjusting [0,2,3]
    w[(0,2,3)] = w[(1,2,3)] + w[(0,1,3)] - w[(0,1,2)]
    t = w[(1,2,3)]
    wp = dict(w); wp[(0,1,2)] -= t; wp[(1,2,3)] -= t
    th = {e: 0 for e in edges}
    th[(0,2)] = -wp[(0,1,2)]; th[(0,1)] = 0; th[(0,3)] = -wp[(0,1,3)]
    dth = {s: th[(s[1],s[2])] - th[(s[0],s[2])] + th[(s[0],s[1])] for s in tri}
    assert dth == wp

import numpy as np
def harmonic(nv, edges, theta):
    D = np.zeros((len(edges), nv))
    for r,(i,j) in enumerate(edges): D[r,i] = -1; D[r,j] = 1
    tau, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(D, np.array(theta, float), rcond=None)

    return h
